articles.title: In just 4 years, Marcos tops 2 predecessors in foreign travel budget, number of trips
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has already made 47 foreign trips, surpassing president Benigno Aquino III and Rodrigo Duterte’s number of trips.

items: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is on a working visit to Singapore from October 7 to 11, marking his sixth trip to the country and bringing his total international trips to 47 during his presidency.

Marcos has surpassed his two predecessors in terms of travel frequency and budget, with a significant focus on strengthening foreign relations and promoting the Philippines as an investment destination.

His trips include various types of visits, with 27 being working visits, and he has received increased budget allocations for foreign travel, reflecting his administration's commitment to international engagement.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will see the skies once again on a working visit to Singapore from October 7 to 11.
He may yet be the country’s most traveled president in more than a decade.

His itinerary to the Lion City includes a meeting with Prime Minister and finance chief Lawrence Wong, the 24th Forbes Global CEO Conference, a visit to the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute, and watching the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix.
This is now his sixth visit to Singapore, his second to the country in 2026. This is also his third time off to the race tracks watching the Formula 1 Grand Prix.
In just his first four years in office, this brings his total international trips to 47, eclipsing his two immediate predecessors, former presidents Benigno Aquino III and Rodrigo Duterte.
Both former presidents were known to have an aversion to foreign travel, especially long-distance trips.
Marcos, who was 64 when he became President, has already surpassed Duterte in international travel budget and is poised to exceed the two past presidents in terms of spending.

Duterte, who was in his early to mid-70s during his presidency, had been vocal about hating traveling overseas. His foreign travel was also limited by COVID-19 pandemic restrictions, with some multilateral meetings shifting online.
Aquino, who was in his early 50s, also hated long trips because he couldn’t stand being without cigarettes for hours.
Presidential foreign trips help strengthen a country’s foreign relations. These trips may also include discussions on the country’s defense, economy, and investments.

Marcos made his first overseas trip in his third month in office. He had seven in his first six months.
The President had the most in 2023 and 2024 at 12 each. In 2025, he slowed down to eight despite receiving the biggest allocation so far. For 2026, Marcos has had eight.
The President has been vocal in his commitment to promoting the country as an investment destination to other nations.
But University of the Philippines Diliman Department of Political Science Professor Jean S. Encinas-Franco said the increase may also be a part of Marcos’ plan to rehabilitate his family’s name.
She added that it may also be a way to diversify foreign allies amid rising tensions in the West Philippine Sea.

“The Marcos administration has decided to engage more with the international community to show that the Philippine government has support from other countries. And also to show that Marcos is trying to diversify the country’s allies,” said Franco.
She also said that the trips will help make the country more visible on the global stage.
“The perception that the Philippines is out there in the world, has many allies, will always show up, or that we are always advocating for our causes or the global agenda,” said Encinas-Franco.
“It’s also important that they get to talk to their potential partners. The government gets to introduce private sector companies who are sometimes part of this delegation,” she added.
The President takes on different types of presidential trips. These vary depending on the level of formality and ceremony. (READ: Presidential trips: What you need to know)

State visits are the highest form of diplomatic visits, with grand ceremonies and meals that honor the relations of the two countries. Official visits, on the other hand, have less grandeur, and a state lunch or dinner is optional. They usually have a smaller delegation.
Lastly, working visits are trips meant for meeting with other government officials to tackle issues that concern bilateral relations.
Expenses in state and official visits are usually covered by the host country. Meanwhile, the Office of the President (OP) pays for expenses during working visits.

So far, 27 of Marcos’ visits are official working visits for international summits and conferences. He also has had 12 state visits and seven official visits during his presidency.

Marcos had an “unofficial trip” to Singapore from September 30 to October 2, 2022. During the trip, he attended business meetings and talked about investments in the country. On the same trip, he was also spotted watching the Formula One (F1) Singapore Grand Prix.
Former executive secretary Lucas Bersamin clarified that the trip was “semi-official.”

Singapore appears to be among the President’s favorites, with six visits. This ties with the United States as his most frequent destination; two were official visits while the rest were working visits.

He visited Washington DC three times to meet with the US president and attend meetings, and once in San Francisco for the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting. He has also been to New York twice, where their family lived for some time during their exile and where he met First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos.
Marcos also visited Indonesia four times, and Japan and Malaysia three times each. These five countries alone account for 46.9% of the President’s reported trips.
Encinas-Franco said that most of the time, the US hosts the larger summits and United Nations general assemblies, which contribute to the recurring trips by the administration.
Since his administration’s first year crafting the budget, the OP’s foreign travel expenses have dwarfed their local counterparts.

In 2025, Marcos received his biggest travel allocation so far at P1.7 billion — P1.6 billion was allotted for foreign trips. In the same year, his office benefited from a P720-million increase in the proposed P913.96 billion National Expenditure Program.
The President’s 2026 travel budget also received an additional P6 million.
Encinas-Franco explained that the additional funding granted may be due to the President’s increased international appearances.

Marcos has already surpassed Duterte in terms of foreign travel budget allocations, based on the General Appropriations Act (GAA) from 2023 to 2026. The President received P3.74 billion from 2023 to 2026, compared to Duterte’s P2.55-billion total allocations for the same period.
Meanwhile, Aquino’s appropriations for his international trips were included in the office’s contingent funds.
Foreign travel expenses comprise the total cost incurred by an individual or office when traveling to other countries for official business meetings, work assignments, and government duties.

Each government agency must fund its own travel expenses from its allocated budget, according to Executive Order No. 77 and Memorandum Circular No. 50. Spending should be cost-effective and not excessive, and foreign travel must meet the agency’s needs and benefit the country.
While there is no official limit for the presidential delegation, the two guidelines require the person’s presence to be critical to the trip’s outcome.
For presidential trips, a cap of two officials per agency is set. Private individuals, spouses or children of officials, and consultants are not covered by government expenses.
During these trips, agencies must allocate funds for pre-departure expenses, daily subsistence allowance, accommodations (room sharing is mandated if possible), and clothing for their delegates.
These agencies declare their actual spending within a period in the financial statements submitted to the Commission on Audit (COA), which is included in the commission’s Annual Audit Report.
Based on these statements, Marcos is on pace to eclipse the two previous presidents in terms of spending.

In 2022, the President exceeded the P201-million budget allotted for foreign trips, spending P396 million. Duterte, who crafted that year’s budget, made no foreign trips in his last six months in office.

However, the president can realign expenses. Article VI, Section 25 of the Constitution states that the president may transfer leftover funds within his or her own office from one line item to another.
COA has already flagged the Marcos administration for over P14.4 million in unsettled funds for foreign travel from 2022 to 2024, covering hotel accommodations and airfare for various agencies.
In 2025, Malacañang said that the office has recovered 55% of the unsettled funds from concerned government agencies. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: This is the Philippines' first Status of Visiting Forces Agreement with a European nation

This is the Philippines' first Status of Visiting Forces Agreement with a European nation

items: The Philippine Senate ratified the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA) with France, marking the first such treaty with a European nation.
The SOVFA establishes a legal framework for the presence and activities of the Philippine and French armed forces in each other's territories, facilitating joint defense and humanitarian efforts.
This agreement is part of the Philippines' strategy to expand defense ties amid regional tensions, particularly with China, while also seeking to reset relations with Beijing.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Thursday, October 8, concurred in the ratification of the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA) between Philippines and France.
With 17 affirmative votes, senators approved proposed Senate Resolution No. 650, concurring in the ratification of the SOVFA, between the two countries.

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and French Minister for the Armed Forces and Veterans Catherine Vautrin signed the SOVFA in March. The agreement provides a legal framework for the presence and activities of the Philippine and French armed forces in each other’s territories.
“This is a historic moment because this treaty ratification of our visiting forces with France is the first for a European nation,” said Senate Majority Floor Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri
Newly designated French Ambassador to the Philippines Donatienne Hissard personally received the resolution at the Senate.

The SOVFA is a “reciprocal bilateral defense agreement that establishes the legal framework governing the presence and cooperative activities of the Armed Forces of the Philippines and the French Armed Forces, including their respective Civilian Components, in each other’s territories, and facilitates joint defense, training, humanitarian, and other mutually agreed activities.”
With the agreement’s ratification, France joins the growing list of countries with visiting forces agreements with the Philippines.

The Philippines has a long-standing Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA) with its treaty ally, the United States. In 2012, a SOVFA with Australia, which has since become a strategic partner of the Philippines.

The expansion of the Philippines’ defense ties has been a conscious push of the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. administration, especially in the face of a growingly belligerent China in the South China Sea. At the same time, however, Marcos has said he wants a “reset” of bilateral relations with Beijing, following years of tensions both at sea and in the diplomatic space. – Rappler.com

articles.title: USS Lincoln carrier to return to port in San Diego after record-breaking deployment – US politics live
articles.summary:
Vessel spent over 260 consecutive days at sea without a port call, a US navy record

As Donald Trump struggled to end the war with Iran, and the Lincoln’s deployment dragged on,…

blocks.text: Controversial record-long USS Lincoln deployment over as carrier set to return home to San Diego
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
The USS Abraham Lincoln will return home to San Diego later today after supporting the Iran war during a record long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea.
For months, there have been widespread concerns since reports first emerged of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health onboard.

In remarks yesterday, however, US defense secretary Pete Hegseth sought to play down the issues, instead condemning “a few folks in the media” who he accused of trying to “turn” the Lincoln’s deployment “into some sort of symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”.

While Trump administration officials pushed back against accounts of poor conditions, families and veterans warned that the length and intensity of the deployment were taking a toll on both those serving onboard and their loved ones.

As reports of conditions leaked out, the Lincoln soon became a flashpoint in the increasingly contentious debate over the war and, for some, a symbol of the strains and pressures the conflict has placed on the US military and the people serving in it.
Hegseth flew out to the carrier on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.
He said that “what makes the US military and the US Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless.”
Hegseth told the crew that president Donald Trump “tracked your activities from day one and couldn’t be more proud of what you executed.”

The US carrier, with roughly 5,000 sailors and marines onboard, left San Diego in November 2025, initially bound for the Pacific and expected to return in the spring. But after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February, the Lincoln was redirected to the Middle East, to support US operations in the region.

As Donald Trump struggled to end the war with Iran, and the Lincoln’s deployment dragged on, reports emerged over the summer of shortages of food and basic supplies, and deteriorating mental health and morale among some crew members, including that two crew members had attempted to jump overboard.

At the time, senior Trump administration officials dismissed the reports. Hegseth claimed they “completely misrepresented” the reality, while Trump, when asked in August whether the deployment had gone on too long, responded, “Not nearly long enough” – a remark that upset some naval families.

The reports about the conditions on the Lincoln caused concern among some military health experts, veterans and families of sailors onboard, and drew outrage from Democratic lawmakers, including several who demanded more information from the Pentagon.
The Lincoln was relieved from its deployment later in August, as the USS George Washington aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East to take its place.

But in recent weeks, as the Lincoln has headed back to San Diego, a new disclosure about the carrier has renewed scrutiny. Acting navy secretary Hung Cao acknowledged last month that eight service members from the Lincoln and its strike group had attempted suicide during the deployment.

articles.title: Russian strike on buses kills 33, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
articles.summary: Ukraine accused Russia of targeting the crowded bus in the frontline city to kill as many civilians as possible.

blocks.text: Thirty-three people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.
Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting a bus carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.
Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Russia is trying to seize as part of Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.
However, Thursday's attack follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across the country and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.

Russia is now launching constant air raids against Ukraine, with sirens ringing throughout the day in the capital Kyiv. According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.

In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack, however rescue officials said the attack caused a fire on two buses that were both carrying passengers.
Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the Donetsk region to move to safer regions of Ukraine.

Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.

Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.

Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".

Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of warned of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.
Such warnings are for now one of the best defences Ukrainians have.
Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.

For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.

Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall. In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.
Kramatorsk City Council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets."

articles.title: Russian attack on two buses kills 30 near Ukraine frontline
articles.summary: Authorities say 18 people also wounded after incident in Kramatorsk in country’s ‘fortess belt’

blocks.text: Thirty people have been killed after Russia struck two passenger buses in Kramatorsk, near the frontline in eastern Ukraine, according to local authorities.

“As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack on buses has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” the Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office said. The governor’s office gave the same toll and said public transport had been suspended.
Images ​posted by police ‌showed bodies ‌strewn across a street littered with debris, as well ‌as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus.

“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” regional governor Vadym Filashkin said ‌on the Telegram app. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”

Moscow’s forces have stepped ​up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and other cities in Ukraine’s so-called “fortress belt“, local officials say, the backbone of its defences in the Donetsk ⁠region.
Russia has demanded that Ukraine cede the rest ​of ​the region still under its ​control before it stops fighting, which ​Kyiv refuses to ‌do.
Thursday’s attack ​came ​a day after dozens were killed in a Russian air strikes across Ukraine, primarily targeting the country’s power grid.
More details soon …

articles.title: AFP evacuates soldier from Ayungin over medical issues
articles.summary: The soldier had a 'prior medical condition,' the Armed Forces says

blocks.text: SCARBOROUGH SHOAL. A satellite image shows a possible raft at the opening to Scarborough Shoal, in the South China Sea, on May 27, 2026.
Vantor/Handout via REUTERS
The soldier had a 'prior medical condition,' the Armed Forces says

MANILA, Philippines — A Filipino soldier deployed to the BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal had to be evacuated Thursday, October 8, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said in a statement.

The soldier, whose identity was not disclosed, “requires immediate medical attention due to a prior medical condition,” according to the military. His medical evacuation — via a rubber boat from the BRP Sierra Madre to a Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) vessel — was ongoing as of Thursday evening.

“The personnel has received initial medical management and remains under observation while arrangements for his emergency evacuation are being facilitated,” said the AFP. The soldier is expected to be on land, at the Western Command (Wescom)’s headquarters in Puerto Princesa, Palawan, before the day’s end.

“The AFP remains focused on the health, safety, and welfare of its personnel. Every necessary measure is being taken to ensure that the patient receives the medical attention and care he needs at the soonest possible time,” the military added.

Ayungin is where the BRP Sierra Madre serves as an outpost for the military in that part of the West Philippine Sea. The Sierra Madre, a World War II vessel, was run aground on purpose in 1999 in reaction to China’s apparent militarization of nearby Panganiban (Mischief) Reef. These days, Panganiban is an artificial militarized island for China.

The AFP has no information on whether the medical evacuation was harassed by Chinese forces, which they often do in flashpoints like Ayungin Shoal. Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea as its territory, including parts that are within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, which is part of what Manila calls the West Philippine Sea. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Nana Patekar, star of Salaam Bombay!, Bollywood films, dead at 75
articles.summary: Nana Patekar, an acclaimed Indian actor and filmmaker, died Thursday at his home in the western state of Goa. He was 75.

image.caption: Indian actor and filmmaker Nana Patekar is shown at an event promoting one of his films, in Mumbai on Sept. 12, 2023. (The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Nana Patekar, an acclaimed Indian actor and filmmaker, died Thursday at his home in the western state of Goa. He was 75.
Indian PM Narendra Modi praised actor's 'intensity, individuality and unmistakable presence'
Patekar died of a suspected cardiac arrest, the Press Trust of India news agency reported, citing a doctor at the hospital where he was pronounced dead.

Born Vishawanath Patekar in 1951 in India's western state of Maharashtra, he built a career spanning nearly five decades in Hindi- and Marathi-language cinema. Patekar was known for intense performances and roles that often portrayed complex or unconventional characters.

Patekar made his film debut in the 1978 Hindi film Gaman and later earned acclaim for Parinda and Krantiveer. He gained wider international recognition in 1988 with filmmaker Mira Nair's Oscar-nominated Salaam Bombay!
He won three National Film Awards, India's highest film honours, and received the Padma Shri, one of the country's highest civilian honours.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi mourned Patekar's death, praising his "intensity, individuality and unmistakable presence" as an actor.
"He brought remarkable versatility and creativity to every role and gave us characters that will be remembered for generations," Modi wrote on X.
Patekar is survived by his wife and a son.

articles.title: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
articles.summary: Casualties have been reported on the vessel, identified by a maritime intelligence firm as the oil and chemical tanker, Acers.

blocks.text: A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
The incident happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal and there were casualties reported, the UKMTO said.

Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers, which was reported as laden with cargo on Saturday as it sailed towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).

The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.
This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.

Vanguard also reported a fire on board another tanker on Thursday in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates. It said the vessel was likely to be the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.
The cause of the fire is unclear and the UKMTO has not reported an incident in the area.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

articles.title: British police charge member of Royal Navy under National Security Act
articles.summary: A serving member of the British Royal Navy will appear in a London court on Thursday to face charges of spying for an undisclosed foreign power.

image.caption: A 24-year-old member of the British Royal Navy has been charged with two offences under the U.K.'s National Security Act, police say. Above, the Royal Navy aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales is shown, before a port call in Tokyo in August 2025. (Eugene Hoshiko/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
A serving member of the British Royal Navy will appear in a London court on Thursday to face charges of spying for an undisclosed foreign power.
Authorities say charges not connected to recent incident at RAF Fairford airbase

Teddy Young, 24, has been charged with two offences under the U.K.'s National Security Act, including preparing to disclose protected information between November 2024 and May 2025, London's Metropolitan Police Service said.
During the same period, Young allegedly obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information for the benefit of a foreign power.
Young has been in police custody since he was arrested on Tuesday at his home in Bedfordshire, north of London. He will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court in central London on Thursday.

items: Former head of German foreign intelligence suspected of 'treasonous espionage'

blocks.text: "These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces," Cmdr. Helen Flanagan, head of counterterrorism policing in London, said in a statement.

"We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter."

Police said the charges weren't related to the recent security alert at RAF Fairford, a British airbase from which U.S. bombers have launched strikes against Iran. Three suspicious vans were discovered near the base in the early-morning hours of Sept. 27, triggering an investigation that has led to the arrest of seven men.
Young was previously arrested on May 21, 2025, and released on bail pending further investigation. His security clearance was suspended at that time and he was removed from his duties.
The Royal Navy issued a statement acknowledging the arrest of a service member.
"As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage," the navy said.

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln scheduled to dock in San Diego after harrowing stretch at sea
articles.summary:
Deployment for nearly a year was marked by reports of supply shortages, and deteriorating morale and mental health among crew

The USS Abraham Lincoln, the US aircraft carrier that has been…

blocks.text: The USS Abraham Lincoln, the US aircraft carrier that has been deployed for nearly a year and has spent months supporting US military operations against Iran, is scheduled to dock in San Diego on Thursday afternoon.

It marks the end of a deployment that has been described as “one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era” and that became marked by a record-stretch at sea, repeated deployment extensions, and reports of supply shortages, and deteriorating morale and mental health among some crew members.

The Lincoln left San Diego last November, initially bound for the Pacific. But it was redirected to the Middle East after the US and Israel launched their war with Iran in late February. The carrier remained there until late August, when it was relieved by the USS George Washington and began its journey home.

blocks.caption: A US sailor on the USS Abraham Lincoln on 9 August 2026.  Photograph: Us Navy/Reuters

blocks.text: Earlier in August, the Lincoln’s deployment made headlines and faced scrutiny as reports began surfacing about poor living conditions aboard the ship, including shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale, and worsening mental health among the roughly 5,000 personnel on the carrier. Two leading military newspapers also reported that there had been two attempts by sailors to jump overboard, causing concern among families and military health experts.

The reports prompted outrage from Democrats, while senior officials in the Trump administration pushed back. Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, called the reports “completely misrepresented”, and when reporters asked Donald Trump if he thought the deployment had gone on too long, he responded: “Not nearly long enough” – a comment that angered some naval families.

In a statement at the time, Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command, claimed that of the US navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln had “among the lowest number of cases related to mental health”. But, he said that “this doesn’t mean that all is perfect”.

blocks.caption: US service personnel of the USS Abraham arrive during their port call in Pattaya, Thailand on 2 September 2026. Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Cooper said that a long deployment at sea “is uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways”.

Two weeks ago, as the Lincoln headed back to San Diego, Hung Cao, the acting Navy secretary, acknowledged that eight service members from the Lincoln and its accompanying strike group attempted to take their own lives.

Sara Jacobs, a Democrat representing California’s 51st district who visited the Lincoln in late September, said in a statement last week that while she is “relieved that the USS Abraham Lincoln will soon be back in San Diego” and “looking forward to welcoming them home” her “demand for accountability won’t end when they make port”.

“I will continue pushing for an OIG investigation into these conditions and a House Armed Services Committee field hearing in San Diego to hear directly from these service members” she said. “We need to prevent this crisis from happening ever again, and ultimately end the Iran war and bring all our service members home.”

blocks.caption: The USS Abraham Lincoln sails toward Chonburi province, Thailand on 2 September 2026.  Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/Reuters

blocks.text: On Wednesday, Hegseth visited the Lincoln ahead of its return, and praised the crew. He acknowledged that their deployment hasn’t been “easy”.

“When you greet your families tomorrow, just pass my gratitude from the president and myself,” Hegseth said. “Let them know that their long wait, we believe, was in service of a righteous and historic mission.”

During his remarks, Hegseth announced that those onboard the vessel would be awarded the presidential unit citation, which, according to the US military, is conferred on units of the armed forces “for extraordinary heroism in action against an armed enemy”.

articles.title: ‘System is rigged’: Democrat Sherrod Brown puts datacenter danger at heart of populist Senate bid
articles.summary:
Ohio former senator attacks Republican rival as the ‘face of datacenters’ as he wraps AI concerns into pro-worker message

Sherrod Brown, the Democratic former senator from Ohio hoping to…

blocks.text: Sherrod Brown, the Democratic former senator from Ohio hoping to return to office in November’s midterm elections, has spent the past year traveling across his home state explaining to voters about all the ways the “system is rigged” against them. Recently, he’s been telling people about a trip he took across the north-west Ohio countryside.

“You’re driving on what looks like really good farmland, driving past fields, driving past barns, driving past milking parlors, and you see, all of a sudden, you see these huge cranes and you see these trucks coming,” Brown told a crowd of dozens at a coffee shop in the city of Lima earlier this month.

The construction site was for a datacenter, Brown said, a component of the AI boom in which Ohio is a national leader. Brown believes the massive installations that pop up without warning do little good for the people around them.

“Nobody knows they’re there,” Brown, speaking in shirtsleeves and without notes, said in his gravely voice, as the crowd murmurs in agreement. “They eat up our land. They swallow up our water … then once they’re built, our electricity prices go up.”

It was the latest iteration of an argument that Brown has been making his whole political career: that the most powerful people in the United States do not have the interests of Ohioans at heart. That message helped him win seven terms in the US House of Representatives and then three in the Senate, even as Ohio grew increasingly dominated by Republicans, and the working-class voters Democrats once relied upon deserted the party.

blocks.caption: A Sherrod Brown supporter in Columbus this week. Photograph: Jeff Dean/Getty Images

blocks.text: In 2024, Brown lost his bid for a fourth term in an election where Ohio voters backed Trump by an 11 percentage-point margin. “It’s not, I promise you, the last time you’ll hear from me,” he said in his final speech on the Senate floor, and months later, he announced another run for the Senate.

Now 73, Brown has made standing up to datacenter developers a centerpiece of this campaign, calling his Republican opponent, Senator Jon Husted, “the face of datacenters”. A report from Ohio’s chamber of commerce found the state gave $2.5bn in tax breaks for the facilities from 2017 to 2024, a period during which Husted was lieutenant governor.
“John Husted, I mean, he’s the guy that – he’s talking like he didn’t now – but he’s the reason these datacenters are here – 200 of them,” Brown said.

Whether the former senator’s message lands with voters is central to Democrats’ hopes of retaking the Senate and blunting Trump’s abilities to get bills passed and judges confirmed for the final two years of his presidency. Democrats must win at least four Senate seats to return to the majority, most of which will come from states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024 – like Ohio.
‘The anchor hanging around Husted’s neck’

Brown has wrapped concerns over datacenters’ impacts into the broad message of affordability that many congressional Democrats are campaigning on nationwide. He peppers his speeches with references to the Iran war, tariffs, Medicaid cuts approved by the Republican congress and rising prices for Affordable Care Act plans brought on by their inaction. Asked in Lima to name an idea to lowercosts if he wins, Brown proposed a new expansion of the child tax credit, which reduced the poverty rate among children during its single year of enactment under Joe Biden.

As the election has drawn closer, Brown has intensified his efforts to tie datacenters to Husted, who Republican governor Mike DeWine appointed in 2025 to the seat JD Vance vacated when he became vice-president. Whichever candidate wins will serve out the remainder of his term, which expires at the end of 2028.

blocks.caption: Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, left, with senators Bernie Moreno and Jon Husted. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP

blocks.text: This week, Brown’s campaign announced a volley of billboards reading “See that datacenter? Jon Husted did that” and a website critical of the senator that offers voters a maps of the facilities in the state.

Amy Natoce, a campaign spokesperson for Husted, accused Brown of lying, saying that while serving as lieutenant governor under DeWine from 2019 to 2025, Husted “did not have the authority to grant tax breaks”. She also noted his championing of the Ratepayer Protection Act in the Senate, which would have required electric utilities toconsider standards that would make datacenters pay for their impacts on the grid. Though it passed the House with wide, bipartisan support, Senate Democrats called the proposal ineffective, and last month blocked its advancement.

“Sherrod Brown and his friends like to talk about affordability, but when the rubber meets the road, they’d rather play politics than actually lower Ohioans’ energy bills. It’s disgusting,” Natoce said.

There’s evidence that Brown’s attacks could be effective. Last week, the New York Times and Siena University released polling that found voters believed Brown would do a better job than Husted would managing the development of datacenters, by an 11-percentage point margin. The race otherwise remains tight, with the Democrat leading the incumbent by three percentage points, within the survey’s margin of error.

blocks.caption: Chris Wright, the US energy secretary, and Masayoshi Son, chair and CEO of SoftBank, at an event in Piketon, Ohio, in March. Photograph: Brian Kaiser/Bloomberg via Getty Images

blocks.text: In August, a memo emerged from the GOP’s Senate campaign arm, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, warning that the issue could sink Husted.

“More than any other thing in this race, datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” the memo read. “If he loses and datacenters get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice – and they will not go near the next one.”

DeWine and his predecessor have sought to encourage the development of datacenters. But political winds have shifted rapidly on the issue – nearly 140 communities in the state have put moratoriums on new constructions, according to the Ohio Capital Journal, and in May, DeWine announced a pause on tax exemptions for the buildings.

Last year, Democrats campaigned against datacenters to gain power in elections in Virginia, New Jersey and elsewhere, and are this year lumping their perceived impacts on electricity prices with the Iran war’s upward pressure on gas prices to argue that Republicans have failed to accomplish Trump’s promise of fighting inflation.
“Husted has been involved in datacenters prior to this election year, and … he’s just more exposed,” said Dan Birdsong, a senior lecturer in political science at the University of Dayton.
It also offers Brown a way to appeal to rural voters who typically do not vote for Democrats, but are sensitive to the possibility of the datacenters being built nearby.
“He has a bipartisan voting base that he can appeal to with this issue that’s different than other issues in the state,” Birdson said of Brown.
Powerful enemies

An Ohio native who received a bachelors degree from Yale University, Brown had been in office almost without interruption from 1975 until he lost in 2024 to Republican Bernie Moreno. By the end of his time in the chamber, he was something of an outlier – the last Democrat holding statewide elected office in Ohio and still describing himself as a champion for workers even amid abundant evidence that they had soured on his party.

blocks.caption: Sherrod Brown, second from right, at an event with President Bill Clinton in Washington in 1998. Photograph: Dayna Smith/The Washington Post via Getty Images

blocks.text: Brown argues that he has the accomplishments to back up his record. As a House member, he voted against implementing the North American Free Trade Agreement, concerned about its impact on Ohio manufacturers, and one of his last votes in the Senate was to pass legislation that boosts social security payments to public employees. Brown has been in politics so long that when Bowling Green State University polled the Senate race last month, a quarter of respondents incorrectly thought Brown was the incumbent.

He’s long courted the alliance of unions, many of whom have backed his comeback attempt this year, though some who supported him in 2024 are now behind Husted. His stances have also earned him deep-pocketed enemies: as chair of the Senate banking committee, he was an adversary of cryptocurrency, and this year, Fairshake, a Super Pac linked to that industry, plans to spend $30m against him, after helping Moreno to victory in 2024.

“We will be outspent for sure,” Brown acknowledged to reporters in Lima, echoing a reality for many Democratic campaigns in a year where Republicans are generally seen as having the fundraising advantage.
His campaign against datacenters also runs up against their own benefits to building trade unions, for which they have provided significant employment opportunities.
Lee Daher, the senior business representative at northwest Ohio’s Carpenters Local Union 351, said datacenters are “a really good source of employment for us”.
“It means a lot of work for our members, not only today, tomorrow, but for the years to come,” he said.

blocks.caption: Brown in Franklin county this week. Photograph: Jeff Dean/Getty Images

blocks.text: His local is backing Brown this year, as they did in 2024, and Daher said his comments about datacenters have not dampened that support.
“They’re coming one way or another, and is there some regulation that’s needed? I think so, but I think big tech is hearing what is being asked of them,” he said.
Asked to reconcile this tension, Brown insisted it was his emphasis on costs that would convince some of the same workers who turned their backs on him two years ago to give him another chance.
“Those unions support me in large part because their members don’t like higher electric bills. Their members don’t like having no say on these datacenters coming to their towns,” Brown said.
“I don’t think very many union members want the state to give these huge tax breaks to these out-of-state billionaires that are building these datacenters.”

articles.title: Supermarket shake-up: why Asda or Morrisons could vanish within a decade
articles.summary: Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons have set industry tongues wagging, with analysts saying the market is ripe for change

blocks.text: They may be two of the most recognisable brands in Britain, with a combined 188 years serving shoppers, but industry watchers agree that either Asda or Morrisons – or both – could disappear within a decade.

This week, it emerged that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons – the UK’s second- and sixth-largest supermarket chains – had held merger talks between last November and February, before the larger player decided to walk away.

News of the potential deal has relaunched speculation that the UK grocery market is now ripe for consolidation and revealed that the Sainsbury’s boss, Simon Roberts – who has been in post for six years – is at least willing to consider the possibility of buying one of his troubled rivals.

Sainsbury’s, which has 600 supermarkets and almost 900 convenience stores, has until recently been seen as wary of trying to revive merger talks with its rivals after its bid to buy Asda for £7bn in 2019 was blocked.
However, industry experts say Asda and Morrisons’ owners have held informal talks with each other – and both with Sainsbury’s team – and predict that talks could restart.

“The three of them, one way or another, are talking to each other,” one said. He suggested that a combination of Asda and Morrisons could happen but was likely to be a weaker deal than a Sainsbury’s takeover of either, as both businesses struggle with costs and interest on debt piles.
Competition fears ease

The industry has undergone significant change since the collapse of the Sainsbury’s-Asda deal. While riding the wider retail trends towards online shopping and convenience stores, the supermarket groups have been jockeying for market share.

Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket, with less than 1 percentage point separating them. Aldi is rapidly opening stores while Asda has struggled to find growth since a £6.8bn, debt-fuelled takeover in 2020 and heavy price competition from the discounters and from its bigger rivals Tesco and Sainsbury’s.

blocks.caption: Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Reuters

blocks.text: Another big change could emerge this month when the UK’s competition watchdog is due to publish its final ruling on whether Aldi and Lidl should now officially be classified as “large grocery retailers” like Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons.

In August, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it had found provisionally that Aldi and Lidl no longer qualified as “limited assortment discounters” as they now carry a “full range” of groceries and operate stores larger than 1,000 sq m (10,700 sq ft) across the UK.
The change means the German-owned discounters are now taken into account when assessing competition in different locations.
This is the strongest hint yet that the CMA has changed its stance blocking the Sainsbury’s buyout of Asda on the basis that shoppers would be worse off.

It also indicates that the CMA’s “balance of competition” – its estimation of the impact of a deal based on drive times for customers around stores – has shifted, meaning Sainsbury’s might have to dispose of dozens fewer stores to gain regulatory clearance for a merger. A figure of 150 was suggested when it tried to buy Asda.

Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital and Sainsbury’s broker, says the CMA preliminary ruling indicates “the shape of the pitch has adjusted a little” and “the change encourages another chapter of consolidation”.

It is a step-change from 2019 when analysts accused the singing former Sainsbury’s boss Mike Coupe and his board of directors of “arrogance” and “folly” for pursuing Asda. Now they say that consolidation is almost inevitable.

That comes amid what is seen as a more welcoming regulatory environment backed by the UK government’s growth agenda combined with the appointment of Doug Gurr, a grocery industry veteran who has spent time at Asda and Amazon, to lead the CMA.
Sainsbury’s holds the cards
One analyst described Sainsbury’s as the “kingmaker” in any industry consolidation as it uniquely has the resources to snap up a rival without the market dominance to immediately prevent any deal.

Analysts agree it is unlikely to face significant competition if it opts to buy Sainsbury’s or Asda – Tesco is too big to buy a rival, while Marks & Spencer and Waitrose appear unlikely to have the financial firepower or desire to pursue such a deal.

Amazon should not be ruled out as a player in consolidation, according to one analyst, who said the online specialist might be prompted into action by any of the supermarkets announcing plans to merge.

blocks.caption: Amazon’s foray into the grocery business didn’t go well and it shut all 19 of its Fresh stores. Photograph: Zuma Press/Alamy

blocks.text: “The last cards are coming on to the table,” he said, suggesting that Amazon might consider buying Asda, Morrisons or even Sainsbury’s, now that it had effectively disposed of Argos which may have caused competition concerns for Amazon.

However, Amazon has not fared well with its dip into high street retail. Last year, it decided to close all 19 of its Fresh stores, with plans to convert five of them into shops under its Whole Foods Market brand.

As analysts at Bernstein put it: “We believe that scale is the most important source of advantage in grocery retail, and the combined market share of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would improve Sainsbury’s ability to take on Tesco.”

The logic of a deal for Morrisons’ American private equity owner is clear. Clayton, Dubilier & Rice has few options for an exit, four years on from its £7bn acquisition of the Bradford-based chain. Private equity bidders are not likely to be lining up, as there is little room for a another debt-fuelled buyout, while pursuing a stock market flotation would require a compelling growth story to lure investors but which is now absent.

The heavy debts taken on to fund CD&R’s acquisition in 2022 have left Morrisons struggling to compete as interest rates have risen, pushing up costs, while competition has toughened as pinched households look to save costs on their grocery bill.

Clearly, the CD&R adviser and former Tesco boss Terry Leahy is unlikely to let Morrisons go cheaply – with price demands ultimately understood to have led Sainsbury’s Roberts to walk away from any deal.

However, Morrisons has fallen back to be the UK’s sixth-largest supermarket with an 8.4% market share, just behind Lidl on 8.7%, according to the latest data from the industry analysts Worldpanel by Numerator.
A ‘sweetheart deal’

Asda’s owners, led by the British investment firm TDR Capital, may also welcome a tidy exit although they are likely to be happier to wait, having largely made their money selling off various parts of the grocer’s assets, industry insiders say. Under the returning boss, Allan Leighton, there are nascent signs of a turnaround if the owners are willing to sit tight and he does not appear keen on reviving talks with Sainsbury’s.

For Sainsbury’s, the appeal is cost-savings derived from larger scale. The combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would hold 23.6% of the UK market and add 500 supermarkets and 1,600 convenience stores to its portfolio – taking it closer to Tesco’s 27.8% market share. Buying Asda would take it to about 26.7%.

blocks.caption: Any motivation for Sainsbury’s comes from the potential cost-savings that a scaled-up merger would bring. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty

blocks.text: One industry expert said a combination with Asda was the “sweetheart deal” because it would not only bring larger scale but involve fewer stores serving the same customers in the south of the country.
The main benefit of any deal would come from cost-savings garnered from combining central operations, such as buying and property management, and aligning supplier terms.

Asda’s bigger supply chain brings greater potential savings and it is arguably a less complicated acquisition than Morrisons, which operates a large food processing business which Sainsbury’s would probably want to dispose of to a variety of specialist suppliers.

One issue is that businesses cannot seek pre-approval for a deal from the CMA, so launching a formal takeover offer for either Morrisons or Asda would involve an element of risk – consuming management time, and costly fees for bankers and lawyers.
As one industry expert says, “the critical argument is the role of the discounters” and the CMA’s rulings do not always follow the expected path. “It’s a lottery,” he said.
Analysts at Bernstein also say that “despite the benefits of a possible deal, the risk of distraction for Sainsbury’s would be high”.

The industry insider says: “Sainsbury’s is best served by being patient” as Asda and Morrisons are likely to continue to struggle. “There comes a point when the CMA has no choice but to let something happen as [Asda and Morrisons] can’t compete. You could argue that is already the case.”

articles.title: [Rappler Investigates] Washing dirty money
articles.summary: Subtext of the revelations appeared to be that money laundering was also in the works. But what types of transactions fall within the purview of the Anti-Money Laundering Act?

blocks.text: Let us count the ways. From what we’ve learned from flood control corruption, there’s the use of casino gambling chips. Remember how Department of Public Works and Highways engineers gambled the hours away, lost a little here, then walked away with stupendous winnings, effectively washing illicit funds collected from irregular activities?

From past investigations, we’ve also learned that real estate is another common method of obscuring the origin of funds, sometimes involving multiple companies and layers of ownership or ownership transfers of estates and luxurious properties. In recent events, allegations of “money laundering” initially flitted in relation to former speaker Martin Romualdez, but Ombudsman investigators are said to still be firming up their case.

Moody’s defines money laundering as the “illegal process of taking money generated through criminal activities and making it appear as though it comes from legitimate sources. Criminal proceeds are usually moved through the financial system using various methods to disguise the illegal origin of these funds, with the intention of using these disguised funds without detection.”

More than a decade ago, Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation got entangled with money-laundering allegations too. Recall the Bangladesh Bank heist and how it seemed like a Netflix whodunnit? Hackers stole over a million dollars from the Bangladesh central bank, with at least $81 million wired to the Philippines. Some key figures got away.

Fast forward to 2026 and we’re hearing of similar methods. Money-laundering experts warn against businesses that involve a lot of cash movements. Think service-oriented businesses or retail, drug trafficking, forced labor, or pig-butchering scams. Others just simply buy lots and lots of expensive paintings, or perhaps even insurance.

Interestingly during the impeachment trial on Tuesday, October 6, one of the insurance resource persons said that, typically, ordinary folks would get up to maybe three, four, or even five insurance policies. The Duterte couple, Sara and Manases, clearly were extraordinary, going by the number of policies they took out for themselves. There were at least 19 held by the couple since 2010.
Subtext of the revelations appeared to be that money laundering was also in the works.

But what types of transactions fall within the purview of the Anti-Money Laundering Act? Business reporter Lance Yu explains that the Anti-Money Laundering Council looks at “covered transactions” by virtue of size (over P500,000 in one banking day) and “suspicious transactions” due to surrounding circumstances. Read more here.

The prosecution has tried to establish too that the Vice President has been less than honest in declarations made in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs), when these submissions are supposed to be made under oath. Could this be the most damaging yet against Sara, given precedence set by the Renato Corona impeachment years back? Read related stories:

items: LIST: Duterte-Carpio bank accounts, balances detailed in impeachment trial
Is Sara Duterte unaware of BPI accounts with father Rodrigo?
Sara, Rodrigo Duterte hid P96M through unutilized manager’s checks — prosecution
Why BPI asked AMLC to delete P2-B worth of transactions from Duterte-Carpio records

blocks.text: If the prosecution winds up with its presentation of evidence this week, the defense should be having its turn next week. There are early indications of the path they will take: distance Sara from both her husband’s transactions and from those of the former president’s.
Is this, however, believable or credible, and doesn’t it violate the essence of the SALN’s intent of accountability, truthfulness, and accountability?
Question is, will the public, which has probably been desensitized to billions of pesos lost from the flood control scandal, still be enraged? Let me know what you think.
Till Thursday after next!

articles.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul.

blocks.text: South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.

But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.

In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.

But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.

After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.

This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.

Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

articles.title: UK scales back Jerusalem consulate after Israel dispute
articles.summary: Britain says its diplomatic mission will remain open with reduced staff, despite Israel's order to close the nearly 200-year-old consulate.

image.caption: Vehicles leave the British Consulate General in East Jerusalem as Britain reduces its diplomatic presenceImage: Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Britain has withdrawn diplomats from its consulate in East Jerusalem after reaching an agreement with Israel over the future of the diplomatic mission.
According to Israel, the consulate had ceased operating in its previous capacity. Britain insisted that the building would remain open under the name UK Mission, Jerusalem.
The move follows a diplomatic dispute over British measures targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
What has happened to the British consulate?
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said 20 British diplomats, including the consul general, were ending their assignments and leaving Israel.
Seven diplomats would be allowed to continue working from the building, although their activities would be "very limited," he said.
The consulate's diplomatic emblem and sign were removed from the building on Thursday.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said London had temporarily withdrawn some staff and their families to ensure their safety.
He insisted the mission would remain independent and operational, continuing to provide "vital services" and work with Palestinians.
Israel’s operations divide London’s Jewish community
Miliband said Britain did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which was established in 1838.
Why did Israel order the consulate to close?
Israel ordered the closure on September 8 in retaliation for British measures against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Britain joined other countries in announcing trade restrictions and sanctions targeting settlements and individuals linked to settler violence against Palestinians.
Israel condemned the measures as a diplomatic attack.
The British consulate has traditionally handled relations with Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, separately from Britain's embassy in Tel Aviv.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in 1967 and subsequently annexed it, a move not recognized by most countries, including Britain.
Miliband said Britain would not take retaliatory diplomatic action while talks with Israel continued.
He reaffirmed London's support for a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
