articles.title: [Pastilan] ‘Walang alam’
articles.summary: If it is not unexplained wealth, as the Sara Duterte defense team asserts and would have us believe, then what is the explanation?

items: Financial records presented at Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial reveal a pattern of suspicious money movements, including P96 million that was obscured through manager's checks.

The Dutertes reportedly held numerous bank accounts, with significant fluctuations in balances coinciding with Sara's resignation as education secretary, raising questions about their financial transparency.
The case also involves potential national security concerns due to large sums of money from China linked to a company associated with Sara's husband, prompting calls for accountability and clarity.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The financial records presented and validated by the Anti-Money Laundering Council and bank executives at Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial this week point to a pattern of money being moved, obscured, and kept out of plain sight.

The Dutertes, multi-millionaires after all, held tens of millions of pesos across a maze of accounts. At least P96 million was floated in financial limbo, shifted into manager’s checks and kept inside the bank while disappearing from customers’ accounts when their wealth had to be declared. The apparent purpose, as presented by prosecutors, was to keep the money out of sight during the filing of their mandatory statements of assets, liabilities and net worth.

Billions of pesos in transactions involving the Vice President and her husband were flagged as suspicious. There are millions more received from China by a company linked to them, given a semblance of legitimacy by purported supplies of banana chips, a rather crunchy explanation for a rather large sum.

blocks.caption: Sara, Rodrigo Duterte hid P96M through unutilized manager’s checks — prosecution

blocks.text: If it is not unexplained wealth, as the Sara Duterte defense asserts and would have us believe, then what is the explanation?

There’s something sinister about money that disappears without actually going anywhere. There’s no robbery the way bank robbers stage it, no getaway car, no maleta stuffed with cash. The money stays safely in the bank, but vanishes from the paperwork.

On Wednesday, October 7, prosecutors presented records showing about P96 million in manager’s checks linked to Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte. The transactions point to a pattern in which substantial sums were kept from appearing in year-end balances.

Consider this: In January 2010, the father and daughter opened a joint time deposit at a BPI branch with more than P40 million. After 12 renewals, it had grown to P41.7 million. When the deposit matured in March 2011, the money was converted that same day into a manager’s check.
Except the money did not actually leave the bank. It moved into a settlement account separate from the customer’s account, where the bank held the funds backing an unused manager’s check.
If the check remained unused for six months, the amount could be returned to the purchaser’s account. Now, if that isn’t hocus-pocus, I don’t know what is.

The money could leave the customer’s account without leaving the bank, then return months later. Nothing really had to disappear in this modus. It only had to stop showing up on the radar, especially at year-end, when the money had to be declared.
Another P55 million was held through a similar manager’s check during the same period, bringing the total to about P96 million.

The defense says Sara Duterte did not know about the transactions because she did not sign them. Let me get this straight: her father could open a joint account, deposit and move P96 million around, and his daughter was simply out of the loop?
Really? P96 million and Sara, the daughter, had no idea?

“Walang alam” (Has no knowledge) is now doing an extraordinary amount of work for the defense. Sara’s brother, Davao Mayor Baste Duterte, used it on the witness stand days ago. And Sara’s disbursing officer used it too.

If everyone involved is “walang alam,” then we have reached a remarkable situation. There are hundreds of millions of pesos, if not billions, mountains of paperwork and transactions recorded by banks and the AMLC, yet apparently none of them knows anything.
So who does?
The documents know. The numbers know. The banks know.
Apparently, everyone knows except the Dutertes.
The bank balances presented a day earlier, on Tuesday, October 6, offer another little arithmetic to think about.

Sara and her husband had at least 30 active accounts across several banks between 2022 and 2025. At year-end, those accounts held more than P59 million in 2022 and over P71 million in 2023. Then came 2024, when the total fell to about P22 million. In 2025, it climbed again, exceeding P35 million.

blocks.caption: LIST: Duterte-Carpio bank accounts, balances detailed in impeachment trial

blocks.text: The sharp contraction came in 2024, the same year Sara resigned as education secretary. She quit in June that year, and her bank balances then took a conspicuous plunge.
Coincidence? Perhaps. But when the dates line up so neatly, calling it coincidence begins to sound less like an explanation and more like an alibi.
Who, exactly, needs 30 bank accounts? And how does someone end up with that many accounts, including joint accounts, without apparently knowing they exist?
Tuesday, October 6, 2026, was a damage-control day for Sara.

As the Senate impeachment court tackled the financial evidence — something the Vice President’s lawyers and husband had desperately sought to prevent — Sara faced the cameras in Davao to attack allegations by former policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., who claims he delivered cash to members of the Duterte family on instructions from a former House speaker.

Between Gracioso’s word and the financial records, the former is far easier to attack from a public relations perspective. A witness can be denied or discredited but financial records, backed by bank executives, are considerably harder to explain away.

The Davao press conference therefore offered a ready-made distraction, shifting public attention from bank documents and figures in the impeachment court to a familiar battle of accusations in the Southern Mindanao city.
With Cale88 Foods, the impeachment case moved beyond unexplained wealth and into questions of national security.

Records show Cale88, linked to Sara’s husband, received P319.3 million from China. Some transactions were flagged as suspicious, and a senator said some firms that dealt with Cale88 turned out to be Chinese state-owned.
China is hardly a politically neutral source of money. It rejects a ruling which upheld the Philippine territorial right while stubbornly asserting its claims, and it has been bullying our people.
Against the West Philippine Sea backdrop, Chinese-linked money flowing into a company associated with the husband of the sitting Vice President raises very, very serious questions.
Why was such money flowing into the company in the first place? Banana chips? And were the entities behind it advancing Chinese state interests? Who was paying whom, and why?
That deserves answers, not evasions.
Convince us, Madame Vice President, that you and your ilk are not Tsinadors — by your words, and more importantly, by your deeds. Pastilan. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Is it better to buy or rent?
articles.summary: Is it better to rent or buy? Try our calculator based on two decades of historical data on property prices, rents and more.

blocks.text: Buyers or renters: Who ends up richer?

Buying a property is the largest purchase most Canadians will make in their lifetime. For many, it’s also their biggest investment. But strictly financially speaking, are you better off putting down a large down payment and facing higher monthly costs as an owner, or remaining a renter and investing your savings somewhere else? Who ends up with more money in their pocket at the end of the day?
Don't miss our simulator below. Keep reading to understand how to use it.

To answer this question, we analyzed over two decades of historical data on property prices, rents, inflation and interest rates across 22 Canadian metropolitan areas, alongside long-term stock market returns.

Using this data, we built an interactive simulator. Every time it runs, it calculates the monthly expenses and financial gains for three distinct paths: an owner with a fixed-rate mortgage, one with a variable-rate mortgage and a renter. Whenever the renter's monthly costs are lower than the homeowner's, those savings are automatically invested in stocks and bonds to compound over time.

The simulator projects these financial paths over a 25-year period across 1,000 unique scenarios. Some scenarios feature high rents and low interest rates; others simulate average inflation paired with weak stock market returns.

The calculations factor in mortgage payments, insurance, property taxes, maintenance costs, condo fees, rent and eventual selling fees. Every outcome represents a possible future based on historical patterns and the options you select.

Of course, no one can predict the future. This tool provides probabilities, not guarantees, and should not be used for major financial decisions. Below is a simplified version of our simulator. You can find a more comprehensive version with expanded options and a detailed methodology breakdown at the end of this article.
Home prices decline, while stocks surge

Our simulator is not perfect. The past is no guarantee of the future, and many macroeconomic factors are bound to change. Canada’s population is aging, the immigration outlook remains uncertain, an AI bubble could crash stock markets and countless variables continuously reshape the broader economy and housing markets.

Because comprehensive historical data is limited, our tool is based on the last 25 years, meaning it does not account for Canada's last major housing crash in the early 1990s. Several experts also pointed out that the cost of maintaining a property is often higher than estimated, especially when a roof starts to leak unexpectedly. Furthermore, realistically, few Canadians stay in the exact same home for a quarter-century.
A sandwich board is shown on a street on Quebec's unofficial moving day in Montreal on July 1. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)
Still, home prices have been declining over the last few years, while interest rates, average property taxes and maintenance costs have increased.
Meanwhile, the stock market has been surging. An investment made in 2005 would be worth roughly seven times more today, compared to just three times more for a property bought at the same time.

Based on this, our calculations reveal a clear trend: If you rent an average studio or one-bedroom apartment and aggressively invest the cash you save by not owning a condo, you have a strong chance of pulling ahead.
But as soon as you step up to a two-bedroom apartment or larger, that math changes quickly. Rent prices swallow up the surplus, making it nearly impossible to save and invest meaningfully.

In fact, in many scenarios, the monthly cost of renting eventually eclipses the cost of owning. A homeowner's largest monthly expense is their mortgage, typically locked in for a five-year term. Adjusted for inflation, the real value of that payment actually decreases over time.

items: Average asking rents fall 4.8% in August as trade war adds fresh uncertainty: report
Why N.S. rents are still increasing far faster than we saw historically for decades

blocks.text: Rents, on the other hand, almost always rise, often outpacing general inflation. Eventually, the lines cross. The renter begins paying more per month than the owner, wiping out their monthly savings and halting any new investment contributions.

Location, of course, dictates everything. In some regions, owning a condo loses the least amount of money after all cumulative expenses, compared to renting a two bedroom or bigger. Buying and then selling a condo is not a guaranteed profit. Single-family houses or townhouses offer a higher probability of financial return, but they come with a much steeper upfront purchase price.
'2 housing crises in Canada'

Yet for millions of Canadians, this debate is purely theoretical, and renting is their only option. Half of all couples in the cities we analyzed do not earn enough to qualify for an average condo in the city they live in — a figure that jumps to two-thirds for a house.
The outlook is even starker for the growing demographic of single-income households. Most Canadians are forced to rent, even when doing so is the less financially advantageous path.
“I would argue there are two housing crises in Canada,” said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

“One is the housing crisis for the middle class, affording a condo in places like Toronto, Vancouver and increasingly in Montreal, especially since the pandemic. But there's an affordability crisis as well for low-income Canadians, who really need help just finding a place to live.”

Affordability is one factor causing younger generations to live with their parents for longer, a May 2026 Statistics Canada study found. They also tend to settle on a career, form a family and buy property later in life, a phenomenon described as “life-stretching.” And when they do finally leave the family nest, they also typically live alone or with roommates more often than previous generations.
This purchasing delay observed among younger Canadian generations can have massive compounding consequences.

“Timing is everything,” said Jean-Philippe Deschamps-Laporte, assistant director of the Centre for Housing and Income Statistics at Statistics Canada, who was involved with the report. When younger generations buy their first property later in their life compared to their parents, this investment has less time to potentially bear fruit.

items: Should you move back in with your parents? Does nothing beat a coupon?
How Nova Scotia became one of Canada's most expensive rental markets

blocks.text: “Younger generations could face returns that are not what they would have had if they had been born earlier."

His own research has found that when people graduate during a recession, it carries consequences for the rest of their lives. The same logic applies to the housing and stock markets. If you are lucky, you buy when prices are low and sell when they are high. But more often than not, you do not really get to choose, he notes, as it depends entirely on your current life stage.
So, should you buy or should you rent?

“The calculations done here are very useful for a lot of Canadians, but the most important thing is to do some introspection on how much owning a home will actually improve your life,” said James Macek, assistant professor at the University of Alberta's School of Business.
Kiana Basiri, assistant professor at the Toronto Metropolitan University, had a similar sentiment.
“We are kind of pushing people toward ownership at the expense of them being tighter financially and less resilient, simply because they really want to own something," she said.
"We just assume ownership is the best way for people to accumulate wealth over time, but I feel we need more education for people on how they can invest their savings in different ways.”
Furthermore, when people move to the suburbs to find more affordable properties, they sometimes forget to factor in other costs, like maintaining two cars instead of paying for public transit.
Fact check: Canadian real estate listings use AI-generated images

As Jean-Pierre Lessard, an economist and partner at Aviseo Conseil, put it: “We are crazy about property ownership in Canada, but there is no link between a nation's economic growth and its homeownership rate.”

A key point he made during a talk in a May 2026 conference was that it’s possible for the average household in Quebec City and Montreal to build more wealth by remaining renters instead of becoming owners.

items: Regina seniors, NDP call for rent control after increases at private retirement community
Toronto board of trade urges province to reform housing regulations

blocks.text: “Originally, public policies to encourage buying were intended to stimulate construction. We've lost sight of that,” Lessard said. “We need to return to something more rational.”

In some nations, it is entirely normal to be a lifelong renter. Germany and Switzerland, for example, are famous for having populations where more than half of all residents rent, backed by robust regulations that cap rent increases and protect tenants' rights.

“Overall, we need to increase the supply of both homeownership and rental units quite significantly,” said ab Iorwerth. The challenge, he said, is to balance supply with measures that encourage homeownership, such as the first home savings account, which tend to push prices up, while simultaneously ensuring there is enough inventory to keep homes affordable.

In June 2025, the CMHC published a report projecting that around 250,000 new housing units would be started each year over the next decade, whereas twice as many are actually needed to restore affordability.
Methodology

The detailed data sets and calculations used can be found here. Our methodology was shared prior to publication with the experts quoted in the article above, and their suggestions helped inform the analysis.
Do you have data that tells an important story you would like to share? Write to nael.shiab@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Dolly Parton's estate has filed a lawsuit against her nephew. Here's what's happened so far
articles.summary: Bryan Seaver, Dolly Parton’s nephew and longtime head of security, is embroiled in a nasty and very public legal battle with the company managing her estate.

image.caption: Bryan Seaver, Dolly Parton’s nephew and longtime head of security, is embroiled in a nasty and very public legal battle with the company managing her estate, which is worth an estimated $450 million US. (A.M. Stewart /AFP/Getty Images, dollyparton/Instagram)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Bryan Seaver, Dolly Parton’s nephew and longtime head of security, is embroiled in a nasty and very public legal battle with the company managing her estate.
Legal battle continues over estate worth estimated $450 million US
At its heart, the dispute appears to be about — what else? — money.
Forbes estimated that Parton, whose death from cancer was announced on Aug. 25, had a net worth of $450 million US.

While neither she nor her late husband Carl Dean had any children, Parton did have a large family — 11 siblings (six of whom are still alive), at least 12 nephews and nieces, according to People magazine, and even some great-nephews and -nieces.
She’s Alive, LLC is the name of the entity created to manage and protect Parton’s estate. It’s run by her longtime manager Danny Nozell.
The estate has also filed a lawsuit and restraining order against Seaver, the family member Parton had handpicked to announce her death.

Bryan Seaver was fired from his job providing security at Dolly Parton's properties, including Dollywood, last month, and ordered to immediately vacate the premises. (Melissa Sue Gerrits/Getty Images)
Want to know more? Here’s how the dispute has played out so far:
Aug. 25: Dolly Parton dies after a brief battle with cancer. Bryan Seaver announces her death to the public in a short video statement on her Instagram account.
Sept. 9: She’s Alive, LLC is created.
Sept. 21: TMZ reports Seaver has been fired from providing security services at Parton’s properties.

A copy of the termination letter obtained by the tabloid indicates Seaver and his staff were ordered to vacate the properties immediately. It says the decision was made "for the protection of the Trust and beneficiaries as a whole." It also states Seaver’s personal stake in the estate is not being terminated.
Sept. 22: She’s Alive files a lawsuit and temporary restraining order against Seaver.

TMZ publishes court documents filed by Parton’s former manager, Danny Nozell, alleging Seaver described himself as an international arms dealer, and raised his military experience to intimidate Nozell into giving him money.
Seaver denies he threatened Nozell, telling TMZ "a lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."
Voicemail from Dolly Parton showed 'how much she cares': Singer
Sept. 23: A Tennessee judge rules Seaver and his company show a "present and continuing disruption and threat" to She's Alive.

Parton’s sister Freida says there is no feud within her family on Facebook. "No one among the Parton/Owens family is fighting over Dolly’s estate," she says in the post. "We all love Bryan, just as we all love each other."

Oct. 2: Seaver asks a Tennessee court to delay a hearing scheduled for Oct. 9, saying he has been unable to find a lawyer to represent him. TMZ reports every attorney he approached had ties to Pinnacle Bank — which is involved with the trust at the centre of the estate battle — thus creating a conflict of interest.

Oct. 5: She’s Alive asks the court to deny Seaver’s motion and submits documents describing how he attempted to evade the person hired to serve him legal documents. They allege Seaver went so far as to put a no-trespassing sign in his front yard and drape barbed wire across the handrails leading to his front door.
Seaver’s next hearing is scheduled for Oct. 20. It’s still not clear if he has found a lawyer to represent him.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Parti Québécois win with record-low vote share revives calls for electoral reform
articles.summary: A record-low vote share for Quebec's incoming PQ government has reignited a long-simmering debate over how the province elects its leaders.

image.caption: Premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon committed to electoral reform during the election campaign. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal
A record-low vote share for Quebec's incoming PQ government has reignited a long-simmering debate over how the province elects its leaders.
With only 28% of the popular vote, party secured 59 seats — enough for a minority government
A record-low vote share for Quebec's incoming government has reignited a long-standing debate over how the province elects its leaders.
The Parti Québécois secured enough seats to form a minority government despite getting only 28 per cent of the popular vote — the lowest vote share for a governing party in Quebec history.
Advocates say the result is proof the province's first-past-the-post electoral system needs to change.

Ted Cragg, a spokesperson for the national advocacy group Fair Vote Canada, said the current model is outdated, particularly in an era of multi-party elections. The group advocates for some form of proportional representation as an alternative.
"We have elections to choose representatives that reflect our wishes, but the system is not reflecting those wishes," Cragg said in an interview.
"It's set up in such a skewed way that people win seats with less than 30 per cent of the vote. Governments now are formed with 30 per cent of the popular vote."
Why the PQ’s victory is reviving calls for electoral reform in Quebec
All five of Quebec's major parties received more than 10 per cent of the vote on Monday, but those results were not reflected in the seat count.
The PQ won 59 of 127 seats, while the Coalition Avenir Québec was wiped off the electoral map entirely despite capturing 13 per cent of the vote.
Québec Solidaire, for its part, won just nine seats with a 12 per cent vote share.
Jean-Pierre Charbonneau, president of Mouvement démocratie nouvelle, a Quebec organization advocating for democratic reform, said many voters feel disenfranchised by the current system.
"People saw the result. We have a National Assembly that doesn't reflect the votes that were cast," Charbonneau told Radio-Canada.
During the election campaign, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said he was committed to electoral reform. Québec Solidaire and the Conservative Party of Quebec have also backed reform.

items: Quebec's next premier promises to hit the ground running as PQ takes power
Electoral reform keeps stalling in Canada, but advocate says it isn't dead

blocks.text: Whether those promises will lead to action remains uncertain.
Both former prime minister Justin Trudeau and former Quebec premier François Legault campaigned on electoral reform, only to abandon those commitments after being elected under the existing system.
Cragg, however, remains optimistic that this outcome could mark a turning point, citing a decade of growing public support for electoral reform in Quebec.
"We take any kind of promise with a grain of salt," he said.
He pointed out that in 2018, all the parties at Quebec's National Assembly, led by Legault, committed to moving forward with some form of proportional representation.
"It does show that there's interest," he noted, "and there's some precedent for the parties to work together."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Benjamin Shingler is a reporter based in Montreal. He previously worked at CTV, The Canadian Press and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal. He can be reached at benjamin.shingler@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Leandro Leviste not yet a ‘fugitive from justice’ — DOJ
articles.summary: The Department of Justice clarified that Congressman Leandro Leviste is not yet considered a "fugitive from justice," despite an active warrant of arrest issued against him by a Makati court.

blocks.text: Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste
Lingkod Legarda Leviste via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Justice (DOJ) clarified that Congressman Leandro Leviste is not yet considered a "fugitive from justice," despite an active warrant of arrest issued against him by a Makati court.

In a press briefing on Thursday, October 8, Office-In-Charge Senior Deputy State Prosecutor Calvin Abugan explained that a specific legal process must be observed before declaring someone to be a fugitive from justice.
“As of now, not yet. We, there’s a process that needs to be followed before we can declare him a fugitive from justice,” Abugan said.
“Also, the court will give him an opportunity to appear before it at the scheduled hearing,” he added.
On October 5, the Makati Regional Trial Court Branch 235 issued a warrant against Leviste and two other individuals over alleged violations of the Public Service Act.
While a warrant of arrest has been issued, two of Leviste's co-accused have already posted bail.

When asked about the National Bureau of Investigation's (NBI) probe into the cancellation of his passport, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said that the direction of the case remains in the hands of the prosecutors.

In November 2025, the Supreme Court set procedures and criteria for declaring an accused a fugitive from justice. The High Court defined fugitives as accused individuals who flee not only to avoid punishment but also to evade prosecution.
Leviste, however, is in France, taking care of her mother, Sen. Loren Legarda, due to a lung illness.
According to a GMA News report, Leviste intends to return to the Philippines and personally face the court to post bail, his spokesperson, lawyer Tony La Viña, said.

articles.title: Study flags ChatGPT for Teens as ‘unacceptable risk’ for children
articles.summary: Common Sense Media says, 'We are concerned that ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails that frequently don't work'

blocks.text: OPENAI. A keyboard is placed in front of a displayed OpenAI logo in this illustration taken February 21, 2023.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
Common Sense Media says, 'We are concerned that ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails that frequently don't work'

items: Common Sense Media assessed OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens and deemed it an 'Unacceptable Risk for all children under 18,' citing failures in safety protections.

The study highlighted that while some protections were effective, others, such as parental alerts for sensitive topics, did not function as intended, leading to concerns about false confidence for parents.
OpenAI disputed the findings, arguing that the testing methodology was flawed and that actual usage data showed limited engagement from teens with the service.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – ChatGPT for Teens, launched by OpenAI in mid-August, promised stronger protections for teen users of the artificial intelligence chatbot. However, Common Sense Media (CSM), a nonprofit which tests and gives ratings to entertainment and technology media, assessed ChatGPT for Teens and called it an “Unacceptable Risk for all children under 18.”

The CSM study, released on Wednesday, October 7, said that while some of the advertised protections held up in their tests, including refusing explicit sexual roleplay, other protections apparently failed or were worse off with the Teen mode setting engaged.
Said CSM, “We are concerned that ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails that frequently don’t work.”

Among the CSM’s criticisms were that ChatGPT for Teens still encouraged engagement even if it posed a risk to the safety of the teen using it. These engagement cues were “pervasive even in crisis situations,” such in mentions of self-harm, psychosis or eating disorders.

Further, parental alerts for teen accounts don’t work as expected, as no alerts were sent when their tests explicitly discussed suicidal thoughts, self-harm, or eating disorder on over a dozen new parent-linked accounts.

Their tests also showed alerts were only sent for accounts “with weeks of sensitive-topic history, which suggests that alerts depend on accumulated account history, not the severity of what a teen says.”

In a TechCrunch report on the CSM findings, OpenAI responded by disputing the assessment and said the group’s testing did not “accurately reflect how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice.” OpenAI also raised concerns about the methodology of CSM’s study.

“Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

OpenAI also released data on Wednesday regarding ChatGPT for Teens, saying use was apparently limited. According to OpenAI, teens spent less than 15 minutes a day on the service on average, with fewer than 2% spending more than three consecutive hours on it. Additionally, teens would take breaks or end conversations with the chatbot within five minutes in nearly half of the instances.

The Common Sense Media study comes amid recent scrutiny of tech company products meant to keep users engaged or using a product or service. Meta Platforms, for one, agreed to pay $18 billion to settle US lawsuits over social media addiction.
The Common Sense Media study, which can be downloaded for free, is available on this page. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DOLE flags labor, safety violations by MV June Aster operator
articles.summary: Authorities are trying to determine whether the alleged violations, particularly in matters of occupational safety and health standards, have contributed to the tragedy.

blocks.text: This handout photo taken on September 11, 2026 and released by the Philippine coast Guard (PCG), shows an aerial shot of the ill-fated M/V June Aster with coast guard boats (L) at the stern off the shores of Coron town, Palawan province.
Philippine Coast Guard via AFP

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) flagged several occupational safety non-compliance and general labor violations allegedly committed by the management of the fire-hit passenger vessel M/V June Aster.

Results from the initial investigations conducted by DOLE’s Region 4B MIMAROPA office were presented during an inquiry with representatives from Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc. at the labor agency’s central office in Manila on Thursday, October 8.
The probe came following the incident in September when M/V June Aster caught fire off Coron, Palawan, resulting in the tragic deaths of more than 70 passengers and crew members.

According to the labor agency, authorities are trying to determine whether the alleged violations, particularly in matters of occupational safety and health standards (OSHS), contributed to the tragedy.

“Ships are built to carry people safely across the seas, not to become their final resting places. The sea may be unpredictable, but the duty to protect human life has never been uncertain,” Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino said.
Alleged underpayment
According to the labor inspector from DOLE MIMAROPA who conducted the probe, initial investigations found that Atienza committed alleged general labor violations worth P665,873.85 in total.

The alleged labor violations include underpaid wages, unpaid overtime pay, unpaid holiday pay, unpaid premium pay on special days, unpaid premium pay on rest days, unpaid night shift differential and non-provision of Service Incentive Leave benefits.
The representative from the management of Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc. said they are yet to verify the presented values.
The human resources representative also mentioned that Atienza continues to pay at least 123 employees despite not having any income for about a month now following the incident.
Alleged safety breach

The alleged OSHS breaches, meanwhile, include the lack of a fire prevention, firefighting, and emergency response plan, as well as the absence of a hazard prevention program, occupational safety and health program, and safety and health committee.
DOLE also claimed that the management’s personal protective equipment was insufficient, adding that there was no trained safety officer and no submitted OSH administrative reports.

According to the labor agency, Atienza management may face fines of around P1,000 and P5,000 per day, and a P10,000 penalty for each incident where a worker sustained an injury due to the cited violations.
The allegations against the shipping company have yet to be proven.

articles.title: Gov't aid amid El Niño might be too late for beneficiaries, says farmers' group
articles.summary: A farmers" group said on Thursday that the government"s response to a potentially strong El Niño could be already late for its intended beneficiaries.

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 3:46pm
A farmers’ group said on Thursday that the government’s response to a potentially strong El Niño could be already late for its intended beneficiaries.
The Federation of Free Farmers Cooperatives, Inc. (FFCI) said that planned subsidies for farmers should be given in cash instead as the government action might take time to arrive.
“Itong El Niño, last year pa pinag uusapan na nila. Ngayon pa lang sila gumagalaw,” said FFFCI National Manager Raul Montemayor in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.
(They have been talking about El Niño since last year. They are only taking action now.)

“Kaya ako naiisip ko, huwag na ‘yung mga subsidy, ibigay na lang ng pera, kung ano mang pera ang available at ibigay sa mga magsasaka. Hayaan na lang ang mga magsasaka na mag diskarte. Kung ano yung kailangan nilang gawin…bahala sila na gamitin, kaysa maghintay sa gobyerno.”

(That's why I think, forget about the subsidies—just give them cash, whatever money is available, and release it to the farmers. Let the farmers figure out how to manage it themselves. Whatever they need to do… leave it to them on how to use it, rather than waiting for the government.)
“By the time na maibigay sa kanila ‘yung mga ayuda, abono, fuel subsidy, tapos na yung El Niño,” Montemayor further said.
(By the time the financial aid, fertilizers, and fuel subsidies are actually distributed to them, El Niño will already be over.)
GMA News Online reached out to the Department of Agriculture (DA) for comment.
The DA earlier said that it sought P45 billion funding to assist farmers and fisherfolk in the looming prolonged drought, which is expected to persist until early 2027.
The request will cover fuel subsidies to farmers and fisherfolk in areas affected by the Habagat and those that experienced drought in the past, mostly in Luzon.

The DA said that it has already begun releasing fuel assistance to registered fisherfolk this week. While mechanized farmers could start receiving the subsidy by the last week of October or in November.
There are 106 areas in the country so far that have already declared a state of calamity due to El Niño. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: DOJ: Vigilance, looking for patterns could prevent potential school violence
articles.summary: "Nag-a-announce muna, eh. Kaya sinabi ko maging mapagmatyag. Si Kuya, si Ate, si Tatay, si Nanay kasi nag-a-announce muna sila bago nila gawin. So may pagkakataon tayo na masawatan 'yung nangyayari,”…

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 3:41pm
Authorities have successfully prevented incidents of school violence from taking place, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said Thursday.

According to Vida, such incidents can be prevented, as there is a pattern in previous incidents where perpetrators would announce their intention beforehand. He cited the three school shooting incidents in Tacloban City, Zamboanga City, and Banga.

“Nag-a-announce muna, eh. Kaya sinabi ko maging mapagmatyag. Si Kuya, si Ate, si Tatay, si Nanay kasi nag-a-announce muna sila bago nila gawin. So may pagkakataon tayo na masawatan ‘yung nangyayari,” he said in a press briefing.

(They announce first. That’s why I said to be vigilant. Older brother, older sister, father, mother, because they announce first before they do it. So we have an opportunity to stop what is happening.)

“At naging successful na tayo. I just cannot give you details. I’ve been receiving reports. I saw reports. I read reports. Marami tayong successful na operations preventing ‘yung potential na incident,” he added.

(And we have already been successful. I just cannot give you details. I’ve been receiving reports. I saw reports. I read reports. We have had many successful operations preventing potential incidents.)
When asked how many incidents were prevented, Vida said the department will consolidate the reports.
Vida also said that authorities continue to monitor “groomers,” but the DOJ declined to give details as this is an ongoing operation.
Justice Undersecretary Michelle Ann Lapuz said that the Batang Ligtas Act was recently approved by the Senate and House of Representatives.

She said the bill expanded the coverage regarding the protection of children to include online recruitment, grooming, inducement of children to commit violent acts, as well as abuses involving artificial intelligence.
Lapuz stressed the importance of a whole-of-nation approach.
“Lahat may kanya-kanyang role dito. At ang batang ligtas, dine-define ‘yung roles ng bawat sector and the accountabilities kapag hindi na perform ‘yung mga responsibilities,” she said.
(Everyone has their own role here. And a child’s safety defines the roles of each sector and the accountabilities when the responsibilities are not performed.)
Lapuz expressed hope that the law will be passed before the National Children’s Month in November.
For his part, Vida called on parents to exercise their parental authority and to do their parental responsibility over their children.
He said that online platforms have tools that will allow parents to be informed about their children.

“Unfortunately, ang laging attitude lang ng magulang, ay hindi ko alam ‘yan. Bahala na siya. So itong mga bagay na ito, kapag hindi i-a-avail o hindi i-exercise ng magulang ang kanyang parental authority, hindi lang ito authority, and responsibility,” he said.

(Unfortunately, the usual attitude of parents is, “I don’t know about that. Let him be.” So these things, when the parent does not avail of or exercise their parental authority, it is not just authority; it is also a responsibility.)

“It’s not just about the authority. It’s about the responsibility. Hindi lang dahil naipanganak na ‘yan okay na ‘yan. Hindi dahil binabayaran mo ‘yung tuition, okay na ‘yan. Kailangan tayong magbantay. Kailangan natin bantayan at kalingain sila at gampanan natin kung ano ‘yung responsibillidad,” he added.

(It’s not just about the authority. It’s about the responsibility. Just because they have been born, that’s not enough. Just because you pay their tuition, that’s not enough. We need to watch over them. We need to watch over and care for them and fulfill our responsibilities.) —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Most UK diplomats to leave East Jerusalem consulate, Israel says, as Miliband says 'vital services' to remain
articles.summary: Israel said in September it would act in response to UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

blocks.text: Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission"

"We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the Consul General would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, but stressed the mission will "work with the Palestinian people".
Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.

The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.
The consulate, which was first established in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.
It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the country had implemented measures announced on 8 September in response to UK sanctions.
"The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed," he wrote on social media.
However, the British flag could still be seen outside and several staff were seen entering on Thursday morning.

Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that "the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel."

But Saar acknowledged that the building is "the property of the British government" and said Israel had authorised "a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity" to operate in the building.
As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, "no steps will be taken against Israel".
Israeli media had been reporting that the UK had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London - raising the prospect of further damaging bilateral relations.
In a written statement on the morning of the deadline, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK does not accept Israel has the right to close the consulate.
"The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory."
Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building "will not be closing" and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from Thursday.
However Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on "necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises".
"Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security," he added.

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 3:02pm

The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday submitted her affidavit to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) regarding dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.'s allegations that he delivered to her suitcases containing millions of pesos in cash.

"Nag-appear na po kami dito by way of special appearance tapos binigyan lang po namin sila ng kopya nung sinumpaang salaysalay, 'yung sinabi po ng ating bise presidente," lawyer Clifford Chua said in an ambush interview.
(We have already appeared here by way of special appearance, and we just gave them a copy of the sworn affidavit of what our Vice President said.)
Asked why Duterte was not present, Chua said that she is not required to appear before the bureau.
To recall, Gracioso claimed to deliver cash to the vice president, Davao Representative Paolo Duterte, and former president Rodrigo Duterte on the instructions of former speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
Duterte read out her affidavit in a press briefing on Tuesday, denying his claims.
Chua said they also submitted the photos presented by the vice president during her press briefing.
The vice president has said Gracioso was motivated by money and resentment towards Velasco and his family.

Velasco's camp on Saturday called out "fabricated attacks" against him, saying these have "no basis." It also called out accusations against Velasco as "inconsistent," tailored as a "one-size fits all" narration.
In an interview on Balitanghali, NBI Director Melvin Matibag said the the bureau will review Duterte's affidavit.

"Kumbaga kung paano po natin tini-treat 'yung ibang mga pahayag na ating pong tinitingnan ay isasalang po natin sa gan'ung standards din kasama na po 'yung mga attachment na ebidensya rito, mga litrato at video, kailangan po natin i-subject ito sa authentication and verification po," he said.

(So, basically, just as we treat other statements that we examine, we will subject it to the same standards, including the attached evidence here, the photos and videos, which we need to subject to authentication and verification.) — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: OVP to seek SC remedy over COA's disallowance of P73-M confi funds
articles.summary: The Office of the Vice President (OVP) Sara Duterte will appeal the Commission on Audit"s notice of disallowance on the P73 million confidential fund disbursement in 2022, defense counsel Michael Poa…

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published October 8, 2026 3:01pm

The Office of the Vice President (OVP) Sara Duterte will appeal the Commission on Audit’s notice of disallowance on the P73 million confidential fund disbursement in 2022, defense counsel Michael Poa said Thursday.
Poa was referring to COA’s 15-page Resolution affirming the notice of disallowance with finality for being non-compliant with the 2015 guidelines on confidential fund use.

COA called the OVP’s acknowledgement receipts "at best, a farce, of no significance, and utterly subpar the scintilla of substance which needed to demonstrate the proper disposal of the OVP's confidential fund.”

“When we filed our motion for reconsideration, we were always hoping for the best but also expecting the worst. So we anticipated that this might have been the resolution of the COA Commission proper, and we've always been ready with that,” Poa said in a press conference.
“Definitely, we will raise this up to the Supreme Court via a petition for certiorari based on rule 65 [on grave abuse of discretion],” Poa added.
Poa said he has yet to talk with the Vice President about the COA’s decision, but he said that they will talk to the Vice President before filing the appeal before the Supreme Court.

“We won’t run out of legal remedies when it comes to the COA Resolution. We will just continue to avail of the remedies available for the OVP and specifically for the persons that were named in the disallowance,” Poa said. --VAL, GMA News
The OVP’s alleged misuse of its P500 million worth of confidential fund is one of the allegations in the impeachment case against the Vice President in the ongoing impeachment trial.

articles.summary:
Foreign secretary says former consulate general will remain independent, operational ⁠and serving Palestinian people

The foreign secretary, ⁠Ed Miliband, has said Britain’s consulate general…

blocks.text: The foreign secretary, ⁠Ed Miliband, has said Britain’s consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​will not be closing but will ⁠be known as a UK mission, remaining independent, operational ⁠and serving Palestinian people.
Israel had ​ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to close ‌on Thursday over the UK’s plans to impose sanctions on settlements in the West Bank.
Miliband said that having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent ​weeks, it would now work to build up its presence.
He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action ​against Israel ​while the ​two sides engaged in ​talks, ‌following speculation it ​could expel some Israeli diplomats from Britain.

Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute.

The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians.

Israel had threatened to close it in protest at the UK’s decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused the governing Labour party of being hostile towards his country.

The ‌incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this.

The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel would be acting unlawfully if it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.
after newsletter promotion

Israel has also said it will revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.

UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis, as Britain became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments thought was unachievable through his methods.

The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believes this is a matter for international courts to determine.

blocks.text: US prosecutors are expected to bring new charges against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans held in Venezuela, a US official said late on Wednesday.
The charges could be announced as soon as Thursday and reportedly concern the alleged wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens during Maduro's 13-year rule.
Prosecutors are also considering charges against others allegedly involved in the torture.
Details of the potential new charges and the alleged victims were not immediately available.
Maduro's wife seeks release
Meanwhile, the 69-year-old Flores is due in Manhattan federal court on Thursday where she is expected to ask a judge to release her from jail and place her under house arrest, citing health problems.
Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds in custody, suffers from dizziness and shortness of breath and may have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
They have proposed that she live at a New York residence under 24-hour security.

blocks.caption: Media reports said prosecutors are also considering charging several other people for their alleged role in torturing Americans [FILE: March 26, 2026]Image: Jane Rosenberg/REUTERS

blocks.text: Prosecutors, however, oppose the request, arguing that Flores poses an "extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released.
They said she has received hospital treatment when necessary, while in custody.
Trump vs Maduro
Maduro, 63, and Flores are being held at a federal detention center in Brooklyn as they await their trial in June next year.
The couple was captured during an unprecedented middle-of-the-night raid on their Caracas home on January 3, which was hailed by US President Donald Trump as a "surgical law enforcement operation."
Critics have accused Trump of operating outside international law.
They were subsequently brought to New York, where they face existing drug trafficking and firearms charges.
Maduro has maintained his innocence, calling himself a prisoner of war and referring to his capture as a kidnapping.

Meanwhile, in August, Trump announced that the US had reached a deal to take control of part of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, which Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodriguez also termed "historic."

articles.title: Supreme Court eases process for recognizing foreign divorces in Philippines
articles.summary: In the high court’s En Banc session on October 7, the Court said the new rules eliminate the requirement that petitioners independently prove the foreign divorce law in court, requiring them…

blocks.text: This file photo shows the seal of the Supreme Court.
Philstar.com / EC Toledo

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has approved amendments to the Rules of Court that streamline the legal process for Filipino spouses seeking Philippine judicial recognition of foreign divorces.

In the high court’s En Banc session on October 7, the Court said the new rules eliminate the requirement that petitioners independently prove the foreign divorce law in court, requiring them only to establish that the divorce decree was issued.

The newly introduced provision under Rule 39 establishes a legal presumption that a foreign divorce obtained between a Filipino and a foreign spouse is absolute and allows the foreign spouse to remarry under foreign law, unless the decree explicitly specifies that it is a limited divorce.
Under the amended rules, the burden of proof shifts to the opposing party to show that a foreign divorce is not absolute.

Furthermore, English translations of divorce documents are presumed accurate if certified under oath by the translator — a presumption that may be contested with contrary evidence, such as certified true copies of foreign divorce laws sourced from the Office of the Court Administrator's central repository.
“These presumptions are disputable, meaning they may be challenged with contrary evidence, under Section 3 of Rule 131,” the Supreme Court’s statement read.

“To challenge these presumptions, Section 24 of Rule 132 allows the submission of a certified true copy of the applicable foreign divorce law, including its English translation, obtained from the Office of the Court Administrator (OCA), which will maintain a repository of foreign laws,” it added.
However, the Supreme Court clarified that the core legal framework under Article 26(2) of the Family Code remains unchanged.
Filipino spouses must still file a formal petition for judicial recognition in Philippine courts.
Furthermore, petitions may still be opposed on established legal grounds, including lack of jurisdiction, lack of notice, fraud, or clear mistakes of law or fact.
Addressing challenges of OFWs

According to the High Court, it introduced these procedural changes after recognizing the significant hurdles Filipino spouses — especially Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) — face in proving foreign statutes.

Citing Department of Foreign Affairs findings, the high court noted that obtaining official certifications and English translations across varied international jurisdictions created unnecessary barriers, which these amendments seek to eliminate.

blocks.text: Senator-judge Mark Villar attends Day 2 of the impeachment trial at the Senate in Pasay City.
Mark Villar via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Mark Villar has regained chairship of the powerful Senate public works committee in his jump to the majority bloc.

Majority Leader Sen. Juan Miguel Zubiri confirmed Villar's switch to the majority during the plenary session Thursday, October 8, where he also announced Villar's election as chair of the public works panel, replacing Sen. Tito Sotto.
The Senate has also elected Villar as a member of the Commission on Appointments, replacing Zubiri.
The majority bloc now has 14 members.
Alongside the reshuffle, Minority Leader Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano was also elected as member of the Commission on Appointments, replacing Sen. Loren Legarda.
Mark's sister, Sen. Camille Villar, remains in the Cayetano-led minority bloc.
Mark previously broke with the minority bloc during the impeachment court's deliberations on whether to do away with the fixed 16-vote threshold for convicting Vice President Sara Duterte.
The senator had voted in favor of allowing the court to interpret with flexibility the Constitution's requirement of conviction by "two-thirds of all members" of the Senate.
Ombudsman probe
Both Villar siblings are facing an Ombudsman probe for alleged violations of the anti-graft law over joint ventures entered into by their former water utility firm PrimeWater Infrastructure Corp.

Besides the two sitting senators, the Ombudsman also named former Senators Manny and Cynthia Villar, businessman Manuel Paolo Villar, as well as PrimeWater executives Fe Reblancos and Romeo Sabater as respondents in the criminal and administrative complaints.
PrimeWater has been accused of entering into deals with local water districts between 2015 and 2022 that were skewed against the government's interest.
The agreements under scrutiny were signed during Mark's term as public works secretary and membership on the board of the Local Water Utilities Administration.

articles.title: UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Thinktank says Britain’s drive towards global commitments is symptom of ‘outdated foreign policy’

The UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic…

blocks.text: The UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic defence, meaning the government’s planned increase in defence spending is likely to result in even greater waste, a thinktank report has warned.

According to an analysis by researchers at the Transition Security Project, Britain has the most overseas-oriented military among European nations, with almost a quarter of the defence budget spent on commitments across five continents.

Calling this a symptom of a “destructive, outdated foreign policy” centred on overseas missions which have often made the globe less safe, the report says the imminent uptick in spending should be accompanied by a change of stance, with a much bigger focus on domestic defence.
The government is committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 amid a defence investment plan (Dip) unveiled in July at the tail end of Keir Starmer’s premiership.
Starmer’s then defence secretary, John Healey, resigned over a refusal to commit to reaching 3% by 2030, but now that he is chancellor that target has been shelved for now.

It would involve a doubling of the defence budget in nominal terms from £70bn in 2026 to £151bn in 2035, according to the Transition Security Project, a research centre which was spun out of Common Wealth, a thinktank with close links to Andy Burnham.

Using figures from 2024/25, the study estimated that about 23% of the military budget for that year was spent on overseas commitments, costing just over £14bn, with the real figure likely to be higher. About £2.8bn was spent outside Europe, including bases in places like Cyprus, Kenya and Oman and elsewhere as “strategic hubs” for projecting UK military power.

The report says this makes the UK the most overseas-committed military among European Nato members, even if France has more personnel posted abroad. The Dip seems unlikely to reverse this, talking about ongoing commitments in a series of continents.
It questions whether more of the new money should be used for domestic defence, and whether the focus on overseas missions has even made the UK safer.
Since 2001, the study said, the UK has spent more than £51bn in modern terms on military interventions in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya and elsewhere.

“Britain’s decision to maintain a global network of military bases and force projection capabilities, combined with high levels of waste in the military procurement system, raise serious questions about how it is allocating public investment,” it says, urging the government to “review its military posture, prioritising defence over the global projection of military force”.

Kevin Cashman, a researcher at Transition Security Project, who co-authored the report, said: “Britain should not pour more money into a bloated military sector geared towards alignment with the United States while Washington starts wars around the world that drive up our bills.”

Khem Rogaly, the co-director of the organisation, and also a co-author, said: “The billions of pounds Britain wastes on global military deployments every year symbolise its destructive, outdated foreign policy.

“Britain should end its support for these attempts at global policing. Instead, it should focus its military resources on defence and its public investment on health, housing and the climate emergency.”
There is an awareness of the importance of avoiding waste among defence officials, including the risk that an arbitrary focus on reaching a certain level of spending could exacerbate this.
The intention is to focus instead on what is necessary – primarily on preparing the UK for a possible war in Europe.

articles.title: Bachelor star Sam Wood denied bail as police allege he choked woman until she ‘thought she would die’
articles.summary:
Court hears police attended Wood’s Victorian home over a similar allegation about three years ago, but the woman had not complained then out of ‘fear of retribution’

  • Get our

blocks.text: A woman who was allegedly choked and assaulted by the former Bachelor star Sam Wood told police she “thought she was going to die”, a Queensland court heard on Thursday.

The court also heard that police in Victoria had attended Wood’s home in relation to a similar incident about three years ago, but that the woman had not wanted to make a complaint at that time out of “fear of retribution”.

Wood, a 46-year-old wellness influencer from Melbourne, was denied bail in a Queensland court on Thursday and will be held in custody indefinitely awaiting trial, after police argued his behaviour was “escalating” and that he posed an unacceptable risk.

Wood appeared in court via video link from the Maroochydore police watch house cells, where he had been held for about four days. He was arrested at Noosa on the Sunshine Coast on Sunday and charged with two domestic violence offences: assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting.

In outlining the prosecution case, police prosecutor Jeanette Grigoris said the brief of evidence included a triple zero call made by a family member, photographs of the victim’s injuries, and a video-recorded statement by the complainant.
Grigoris said the complainant was supportive of the charges proceeding.
Wood’s lawyer has indicated the reality TV star will fight the charges.
The court heard that in the video statement, the woman alleges she was choked and that “there was a cessation of breath”.
“She articulates the banging of her head on the floor. She couldn’t breathe,” Grigoris said.
“She thought she was going to die.”
Grigoris said the video statement by the woman also refers to a previous matter in Victoria “being of a similar nature” and “involved choking”.
The court heard that in a police interview, recorded about midnight on Sunday morning.
Wood denied that any previous incident had taken place in Victoria.
Grigoris said there was body-worn camera footage of police attending his home and a police report in relation to that incident.
Grigoris said the woman “did not make any criminal complaints on that occasion, she was in fear of retribution of the defendant.”
Grigoris also raised concern that Wood, during his police interview, minimised his part in the alleged offending, and minimised the injuries suffered by the woman.
“He’s essentially victim blamed,” she said.
Wood’s lawyer, Matthew Cuskelly, sought bail and said his client denied the allegations. He cited a psychologist’s report that said Wood was suffering from “severe depression”.
“He ought to be given the opportunity to engage with mental health professionals,” Cuskelly said.
“And also try to salvage something of his professional reputation and career, which is taking a hell of a beating at the moment.

“Ultimately, as all families have, there was problems. And my client had been enduring the hardship of attempting to quarantine those problems from his family for some period of time. It was agonising.”
Cuskelly cited a psychologist’s report that describes ‘the difficulty that my client has been enduring in respect of the deterioration of his psychological state”.
“His depression is regarded as extremely severe.”
Cuskelly said Wood had no prior criminal history and if granted bail would reside in Victoria with his father, Andrew Wood, who attended the court in support of his son.
Acting magistrate Janelle Boegheim said she was not satisfied by the defence argument that the case against Wood was weak.
“The strength of the evidence against the defendant is … relatively strong at this juncture.”
Boegheim said it was likely the charges, if proven, would attract a term in prison.
Wood was stood down by his own fitness empire, 28 by Sam Wood, on Monday, a day after he was charged.
“We have all been shocked and saddened by the matters involving Sam Wood,” said Mark Watkin, the group’s acting chief executive.
“We have zero tolerance for domestic violence. While the matter is under investigation and before the court, Sam is on indefinite leave from his duties.
“Our thoughts are with the family and anyone in the community affected by domestic violence.”
He is due to face court again on November 23.

articles.title: Thursday briefing: Why young people are taking to the streets across France
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: A youth-led movement is protesting crumbling school buildings and teacher shortages while turning adult focus onto wider educational inequalities

Good morning.…

blocks.text: Good morning. In my experience, at any protest, the most memorable and encapsulating slogans are always the ones written by hand with marker pen on cardboard placards.

“School is a right, not a privilege,” read one such sign held aloft by a student in Paris, where huge youth protests over the state of high school education have brought tens of thousands of young people and adults on to the streets, with further strikes planned today.
“A state that gasses high school students is a weak state,” another sign said, referencing growing public anger at alleged police brutality towards young protesters.

Tens of thousands of young people have also taken to Spanish streets in recent weeks to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis. And outside the Labour conference in Liverpool last week, a crowd of jobless young people protested against what they saw as their bleak employment prospects. From Paris to the north of England, a similar thread runs through it all: a generation who feel betrayed by the absence of basic economic security and the erosion of public services that older generations took for granted.
I spoke to our Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis who has been reporting from the centre of the French protests. But first, the headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK politics | Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich.

Education | Labour’s flagship changes to special education in England are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, new analysis has found.
Spain | María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died.
Science | A type of gene therapy based on Nobel prize-winning science is safe and can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers have revealed.
Epstein | British billionaire Sir James Goldsmith warned that Jeffrey Epstein was a “sexual deviant” decades before the FBI closed in on the abuser, a Guardian investigation has found.

blocks.text: In depth: Why have young people taken to the streets?

blocks.caption: ‘School is a right, not a privilege’ … students take to the streets in Paris. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

blocks.text: The most significant youth movement to emerge across France in recent decades started on 17 September. Pupils returning to the Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, southwest of Paris, after the summer holidays, discovered they couldn’t continue their studies because of the extent of staff absences. The 15- to 18-year-olds blockaded their high school in protest.

After negotiations with the education ministry, those staffing gaps were filled, but the impassioned complaints about crumbling buildings, overcrowded classrooms, and long school days – alongside a wider sense of inequality in the education system – resonated in the suburbs. “This movement grew from the ground up, from teenagers speaking to others outside their lycées. And over a couple of weeks, it has spread to hundreds of schools across France,” Angelique tells me.

There’s a tendency to mythologise youth protest, especially in France – my uncle Joss was in Paris in 1968, and I lapped up his tales of pulling up cobblestones with his bare hands to build barricades. But youth activism is often diminished. When I reported on the schoolchildren who protested against the war in Iraq in 2003, and those who took part in climate strikes more than a decade later, adults repeatedly questioned whether they were swayed by older provocateurs or just wanted an excuse to dodge school and indulge in petty vandalism. (In my experience: no, no and no.)

So it is in France this past month. “This is very much a youth movement,” says Angelique, comparing it to similar protests in 2006 over an unpopular youth employment contract, which were organised by students’ unions. “High schoolers are organising themselves without a centralised system or even spokesperson. That’s historic, and it’s taken the government by surprise.”
Who are the teenagers on the streets?

This week, the sociologist Fabien Truong, who has written widely on youth protest culture, praised the “maturity and coherence” of the protesters. He pointed to a “social media effect” whereby teenagers in wealthier areas were sharing videos of scurrying rats, gaping ceilings and leaking toilets in poorer schools. “It’s beautiful, this solidarity with students from more privileged backgrounds fighting for others and more equality.”

This is precisely what Angelique has witnessed on the streets of Paris in recent days, where some of the most elite state schools have also been barricaded. She spoke to one teacher outside a school in a richer inner-city area, who was proud of her pupils. “She said there was a feeling of solidarity and generosity between teenagers, and how it flies in the face of the idea that they’re part of a social media generation who are selfish and narcissistic.”

“I spent a long time speaking to teenage girls at one of the barricades in the centre of the city,” Angelique says,“who were sitting on top of a pile of bins and shopping trolleys. They told me: ‘We’re told in France that state education is a great leveller, but that’s not the case. We are being taught our lessons, but we’re getting out on to the street because we can’t bear to know that other students in poorer areas are in buildings that are crumbling’.”

***What’s wrong with French schools?As Angelique sets out in this helpful explainer, the pupils’ grievances are backed up by evidence – and the prime minister himself has described them as “legitimate”. Thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, are in need of repair. Class sizes are bigger on average, and school days are longer, than in other comparable countries, while about 10% of teaching hours across the year are not delivered because of absent teachers.

And yet France’s expenditure on high schools is 28% higher than the OECD average. What’s going on? The high spend can be explained in various ways, Angelique tells me. France has a lot more high school buildings to maintain than other countries, and many more vocational courses that cost more to teach.

At the same time, more spending is desperately needed on staff. Teacher shortages are linked to very low pay progression through the profession, while there are severe difficulties in finding teachers to work in deprived areas. There’s also a shortfall in other crucial roles, including school nurses and support staff for pupils with disabilities.
How have adults responded?

Angelique tells me that what has defined how adults are responding to this burgeoning movement is the behaviour of politicians and police. Initially, the French government “had its head in the sand”, she says, distracted by public anger at rising fuel costs and a difficult budget process. “And when it suddenly woke up, the reaction was not a political one, it was a police crackdown.”

Eighteen investigations into possible police brutality are already under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after contact with a stun grenade and a 14-year-old whose jaw was shattered after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher.

Yesterday, the French interior minister suspended the use of stun grenades but rejected accusations of police brutality, saying riot officers only intervened when protesters turned violent. Dozens of teachers have also been injured in clashes, and a small number of schools burned or ransacked, but Angelique tells me that most protests have been peaceful.

The injuries, however, have prompted outrage, with parents and teachers angry at the “disproportionate police response” now joining young people at the barricades. An Elabe poll for BFMTV, published on Wednesday, found that 72% of French people thought the student’s demands were legitimate – although 55% of of those surveyed also thought the protests should come to an end.

The movement has also brought to the fore a debate about the wider state of public services ahead of next year’s presidential election. The radical left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, backed for president by 47% of voters under 35, is loudly supporting the protesters, while far-right candidate Marine Le Pen has blamed the current government for chaos and called for an anti-riot law.

The sheer scale of the marches in cities across France this week was unexpected, Angelique says. “There were hundreds of thousands of parents, grandparents and teachers. There is a lot of support for these young people’s demands and an understanding that the problems they are raising reflect wider worries about public services.”

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Luis Gómez, known as JM, sings with Los Cracks del Puerto at the SCD Hall in Santiago, Chile. Photograph: Tamara Merino/The Guardian

blocks.text: At 65 years old, Luis Gómez was still hawking vegetables at the market he had worked at since the age of eight. Now at 80, Gomes, or JM as he is popularly known, has become a musical sensation, selling out venues across Chile, as well as in Mexico, the UK, Argentina and France. He is the frontman of Los Crack del Puerto, who in May released their fourth record, Lo Mucho Que Nos Queda (So Much Yet to Come), as a cassette – to great acclaim.

It’s a long way from his early life in the city of Valparaíso; the youngest of five children, he was three when his father died, and 10 when he lost his mother. For a time, he slept on the street between parked cars. JM would eventually form a musical double act with his cousin, Juan Navarro, and the two entertained crowds in Valparaíso’s bars. The pair would find fame well into their 70s after forming the band in 2017. “I never planned any of this, and I’d be happy still working at the market,” JM says. “But I suppose it’s never too late to give something a try.”
