articles.title: Woman at centre of Cornell gang-rape case was 'misled' about investigation, lawyer says
articles.summary: The woman who says several men raped her at a Cornell University fraternity party was "misled" about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said…

image.caption: Cornell's police department gave the woman at the centre of gang-rape allegations the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, her lawyer says — but the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began. (Matt Burkhartt/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The woman who says several men raped her at a Cornell University fraternity party was "misled" about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said Wednesday.
Criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began, but Jane Doe was given impression it was ongoing: lawyer

Even as she took her allegations about a 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity house through Cornell's internal disciplinary process, the university's police department gave her the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, lawyer Thomas Giuffra told The Associated Press.
In fact, the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began.

Tompkins County district attorney Matthew Van Houten, the local prosecutor, made the decision not to go forward with a criminal case within days of the woman giving her first substantial interviews to police.

items: Allegations in Cornell 7 case fit pattern of institutional failure on sexual assault, says sociologist

blocks.text: Van Houten has said he asked Cornell's police department to convey the decision to the woman, who is referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, but never spoke personally to her or her lawyer.
Giuffra said the woman was told the criminal investigation was ongoing.
"I think she was misled," he said. "I was involved with this case early on. I thought they were still investigating. It was news to me that they weren't doing anything."
At the time, Giuffra added, he assumed investigators just needed more time to speak with witnesses and build a case.
"But nothing was being done, and we didn't know that," he said.
A messages seeking comment was left for Van Houten. Cornell's media relations office, citing pending litigation, declined to comment on behalf of the university's police department.

The district attorney said in a statement last week that he was confident no further investigation was necessary after prosecutors and criminal investigators from his office reviewed a six-page summary of the woman's account, written by a police officer.
'Cornell 7' lawsuit: What we know
Different accounts
Based on that summary, Van Houten said he believed no crime had been committed, and that the woman's participation in drug use and sex was "voluntary, conscious and consensual."

That description differs sharply with what the woman told police and university investigators, and with what she alleged in a lawsuit filed against seven Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell and others last month.

Among other things, Giuffra said, the six-page report omitted the woman telling investigators, "I can say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped," that she was subjected to physical violence, and that a fraternity brother had sent a message to a group chat using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman's body was freely available.

Last week, citing investigative records it obtained, the New York Times reported that a Cornell police investigator tried to get Van Houten's office to consider additional evidence in the weeks after the alleged rape, but was rebuffed.
"At first I thought these police were incompetent," Giuffra said. "It sounds like they were doing the right thing. And they just got shut down."

Giuffra said while he and Jane Doe have received death threats, he has been heartened by an outpouring of support — including rallies and protests on the Cornell campus and more than 1,000 women who have emailed him to share anger, frustration, solidarity and stories of their own assaults.
Cornell students protest university handling of sexual assault case
Case taken away from Van Houten

Jane Doe, who was a student in 2024, alleges that Chi Phi members plied her with alcohol and drugs and several of them sexually assaulted her. One man sent others a message inviting them to participate, according to a lawsuit she filed last month.

Lawyers for two of the men have denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the others or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Some of the men who underwent a university disciplinary hearing in 2024 told investigators that the sexual activity was consensual or said they were not involved.

The woman went to Cornell police in November 2024, though no criminal charges resulted. In the wake of her lawsuit, Van Houten said he was reopening the investigation. Days later, Gov. Kathy Hochul took the case away from him and appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor.

items: Jane Doe at centre of Cornell rape case targeted with threats, her lawyer says
Cornell taps ex-Justice Department official Sally Yates to review school's handling of sexual assault cases

blocks.text: Giuffra applauded the move, saying he was troubled by Van Houten's plan for conducting the reopened investigation and "didn't think he was up to the task."
Giuffra said the district attorney wanted to take the case to a grand jury and have Jane Doe testify before the panel within two weeks.

That timeline, leaving little time to review evidence or interview witnesses, suggested Van Houten may have been trying "to go take a dive and not really give it his best effort and not do any investigation," Giuffra said.
James hasn't said how long her investigation might take, but suggested it could be months.

On Wednesday, one of the men named in Jane Doe's lawsuit filed a court petition seeking James's removal from the case, arguing she showed bias by posting on social media a few days before her appointment: "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable."
A spokesperson for James declined to comment.
Cornell closed down the Chi Phi campus chapter in 2024 and says it expelled some students and suspended others after an investigation under the federal Title IX law.

This week Cornell trustees brought in former U.S. deputy attorney general Sally Yates to review how the school investigates sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the campus police response and more.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Bookmark this page for Rappler's comprehensive coverage of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial at the Senate

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

blocks.caption: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte

blocks.text: LATEST UPDATES

Is Sara Duterte unaware of BPI accounts with father Rodrigo?

What did the defense team — and the Vice President, for that matter — accomplish in claiming that Sara Duterte had no knowledge of the joint bank accounts with her father, who was detained in The Hague? House prosecutor Terry Ridon had a response that mirrored the thought balloon of many trial observers that day: “Magandang araw po, Pangulong Duterte. Nilalaglag po kayo rito.”

articles.title: Jurors in Beau Lamarre-Condon murder case shown photos of decomposed bodies
articles.summary:
Former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to the February 2024 murders of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Sydney

  • Get our

blocks.text: Photographs of the decomposed bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies have been shown to 15 jurors tasked with deciding whether the two men were murdered.
Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to the February 2024 murders of Baird, 26, and Davies, 29.
The third week of his double murder trial has pivoted to how investigators found the remains in rural NSW.

Retired crime scene officer Greg Moon, who coordinated the forensic sweep of the Greek monastery at Bungonia where the men’s bodies were found, continued giving evidence on Thursday about the condition of the remains.
Most of the family members of Baird, a former TV presenter, and Davies, a Qantas flight attendant, have not been present in court for the grisly forensic evidence.
Justice Natalie Adams warned jurors on Thursday they would see confronting photos of decomposition.
The bodies were discovered inside two surfboard or stand-up paddleboard bags, with the smaller bag containing the body zipped up inside a larger one, Moon said.
Moon said the bodies were discovered one on top of the other with rocks and small branches placed on top.

blocks.caption: Evidence and testimony in week two of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s trial – video

blocks.text: Fellow investigator Christine Abela said she immediately knew something was amiss when she first arrived at the rural property more than a week after the two men were killed in the summer of 2024.
“There was a strong smell as soon as I got out of the car,” she told a NSW supreme court jury on Wednesday.
“The scent of a decomposing body.”
Abela detailed how investigators found concrete blocks, a gym weight and a cut padlock at Cella Farm, where Lamarre-Condon allegedly unsuccessfully attempted to sink the bodies in a dam.
after newsletter promotion
Moon said there were multiple indicators that the remains had been at the monastery, about 20km away from the farm, for several days.
“A large number of maggots and other insects were present in the bags along with other decompositional fluids,” he said.
Lamarre-Condon’s efforts to clean up and dispose of Baird and Davies’ bodies have come under scrutiny during the trial.
His barrister says the actions to dispose of their bodies at Bungonia, 200km south of Sydney, were indicative of his panic about the unexpected deaths.

Earlier in the trial, jurors were shown CCTV of the alleged actions the senior constable took in the hours after the killings, including buying a second surfboard bag and hiring a larger second vehicle.
The footage, released by the court on Thursday, allegedly shows the heavily disguised Lamarre-Condon returning to the alleged murder scene laden down with cleaning products and a tarpaulin.
The 12-week trial continues.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Oct. 7: VP and husband's millions
articles.summary: A record-breaking fifteen executives from banks and insurers took the witness stand in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday, October 7, to authenticate documents that…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A record-breaking fifteen executives from banks and insurers took the witness stand in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday, October 7, to authenticate documents that attest to her and her husband's alleged wealth.

Article II charges Duterte with amassing wealth disproportionate to her lawful income and failing to fully and truthfully disclose her and her husband Manases Carpio’s assets in her SALNs (statements of assets, liabilities and net worth) for 2022, 2023 and 2024.
It also accuses her of failing to divest from businesses, as the Constitution requires of the president and vice president.

In calling the bank and insurance witnesses, the prosecution sought to put on record the year-end balances in the couple’s accounts, so it can compare each year’s balance against the SALN for the same year.
Prosecutors have argued the records are meant to establish a baseline of Duterte’s wealth and a “pattern of non-disclosure.”

The marathon hearing on Wednesday laid out two clashing ways of reading Duterte’s finances. It's the prosecution's argument that there are serious indications of undeclared wealth just by comparing the SALN and bank balances alone. Citing bank records, the prosecution has pointed out that the Duterte couple had P59 million in bank balances at the end of 2022, her first year in office, against P13.325 million in declared “other personal properties.”

The defense, meanwhile, has countered that transactions from before she took office are irrelevant and that not all the transactions being wielded as evidence by the prosecution were signed off by Duterte herself.
Duterte and her husband have more than 30 to 40 total bank accounts across eight different banks, according to the prosecution.
Here are the three highlights from the proceedings on October 7.
1. The ‘tinikling’ manager’s checks

A bank executive told the court that P41.7 million from a time deposit in the names of Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, was repeatedly moved into bank-issued checks in 2011.

Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) division head Marvin Galvez testified that the money started as a P40.65-million time deposit opened in January 2010. By March 9, 2011, the amount had matured to P41.72 million after the interest had accumulated during several rollover periods. On this day, the funds were moved to the Dutertes' joint account at BPI’s Julia Vargas branch.

The same day, the full amount was used to buy a manager’s check, a check guaranteed by the bank and valid for six months. After that check lapsed, another for the same amount was bought on Oct. 20, 2011.

Upon questioning, Galvez confirmed that money held in a manager’s check leaves the depositor’s account but does not appear in the year-end balance. Instead, it is moved into the bank's internal settlement account, making it the bank's liability.

Because of this, prosecutors pointed to the checks as a way of bypassing the SALN by keeping the money in limbo, given public officials are required to declare their cash on hand or in bank, among others, when they file the document by the end of each year.
Private prosecutor James Bryan Alih said the money moved this way for “three or four years.” He said a second deposit, of P55 million, was handled the same way, bringing the total to P96 million.
Galvez’s records also showed four transfers of P20 million each from the Dutertes' joint account to BPI-Philam Life on March 28, 2014, for insurance plans worth P80 million in total.
A P16.85-million manager’s check from the same account was made out to "Samuel C. Uy" in May 2016, according to documents read out in court.

Sen. Tito Sotto, in his interjection, compared the alleged scheme to tinikling, the folk dance in which dancers dodge clapping bamboo poles. When Sen. Bam Aquino asked if it was a "known practice" among bankers, Galvez said it was “not uncommon” for clients to return unused checks.
Galvez said he could not tell the extent to which clients do it on purpose, but noted that purchasing managers' checks require them to state their reason for doing so in the application form.
Defense counsel Michael Poa claimed Duterte had no knowledge of the BPI joint account she had with her father and was only made aware of it during prior House hearings.

The joint account was also structured in a way that only the elder Duterte could transact alone, Poa pointed out, while Sara Duterte as co-depositor required her father's permission to move around any funds.
Poa also noted that the BPI records presented during the trial, including the P41.7-million manager's check, bore the signature of the former president and not Sara Duterte.
2. Millions in the bank, year after year
Bank witnesses put the couple’s combined year-end balances across eight banks at the following amounts, as summarized by the prosecution:

items: 2022: P59 million
2023: P71.3 million
2024: P22.2 million

blocks.text: On the flip side, the vice president declared zero cash on hand or in the bank for her SALNs from 2022 to 2024.
But the defense has long sought to debunk the allegation that Duterte misdeclared her wealth by explaining that cash on hand was grouped under "others" or "other personal properties" in her SALNs.

Based on the bank records cited by the prosecution, however, the Duterte couple's 2022 year-end balance of P59 million is more than four times the P13.325 million that was declared in “other personal properties” in the SALN that year.
Under cross-examination, the bank witnesses said they had no personal knowledge of the accounts and testified only from records produced under subpoena.

The Duterte couple kept at least 30 active accounts across eight banks from 2022 to 2025: LandBank, AUB, PSBank, Metrobank, Security Bank, BPI, PNB and BDO. These include accounts held jointly with other family members.
At BPI alone, Galvez counted seven active and 34 closed personal accounts, plus two credit card accounts and one corporate account.
3. Did Security Bank flag Cale88 transactions as suspicious?

Security Bank official Leslie Cham testified that Cale88 Foods Corporation, a declared business interest of Carpio, kept two peso checking accounts with the bank. One was opened in August 2024 and the other in October 2025. Both were closed in July 2026, the month the trial began.

Cham said Cale88’s account recorded P40.14 million in inflows and P40 million in outflows in 2024, and P6.27 million in inflows in 2025. The two accounts closed with balances of P332,530.95 and P21,164.27.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian then read from suspicious transaction reports on Cale88 as provided by the Anti-Money Laundering Council:

items: There were 12 cash deposits flagged as not matching Cale88 declared financial profile
Cale88 was flagged for failing to provide supporting documents and stopped responding to requests for clarification, so the bank could not verify where the money came from or what it was for.

blocks.text: Asked whether it was Security Bank that filed those reports, Cham said: “I cannot confirm.”
Cham invoked the confidentiality clause of the Anti-Money Laundering Act and said he could not say whether suspicious transaction records were indeed filed on Cale88.

Corporate records identify Cale88 as a Davao-based banana chips exporter. But the prosecution previously raised red flags about the firm, such as its low reported electricity bills, unusual for a food factory, as well as its large inward remittances from Chinese companies.
October 7 was the longest trial day yet, surpassing the previous record holder just two days before, which lasted around nine hours.

articles.title: Brazil: Thousands of students march against Bolsonaro
articles.summary: After Flavio Bolsonaro came out on top in the first round of Brazil's presidential election, thousands of people joined student-led protests against the far-right in Rio de Janeiro.

image.caption: Thousands of students took to the streets of Rio de Janeiro in protest against Flavio BolsonaroImage: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: Thousands of people joined a student march in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on Wednesday to protest against the possibility of Flavio Bolsonaro becoming president after the far-right candidate came out on top in the first round of the country's presidential election on Sunday.
Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, won around two million more votes than the incumbent president, the left-leaning Lula da Silva.
But since neither reached the 50% hurdle to win the presidency, the pair will face off in a run-off on October 25, in which Bolsonaro is considered the favorite.

blocks.caption: 'No to Flavio and yes to education,' read one signImage: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: "If Bolsonaro wins, Brazil will become a colony of the United States," said 20-year-old literature student Joao Victor Vieira, voicing the fear of many on the left in Brazil that Bolsonaro is too ideologically aligned with US President Donald Trump.
Brazil: 'Never again Bolsonaro'

Other marchers held signs with messages such as "Brazil isn't anyone's backyard," "I don't vote for someone who sells Brazil," and "Never again Bolsonaro" – all against a soundtrack of drums, fireworks and chants.

blocks.caption: 'Brazil is not the backyard of the US,' read one protester's signImage: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We're fighting for Brazil, not for Lula," said Talita Amaral, a 19-year-old environmental sciences student, wearing Brazil's iconic yellow and green football shirt, often worn by nationalist Bolsonaro supporters but which opponents have been aiming to reclaim for themselves.
"We don't have time to be sad, we need to be doing this, occupying the streets, sending messages in WhatsApp groups, trying to convince people," she told the Associated Press.

blocks.caption: 'Fascists in jail, people in the streets,' this protester wrote on a Brazilian flagImage: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: For Alice Carneiro, a 25-year-old maritime shipping administrator, the prospect of another Bolsonaro conjures fears of far-right policies which will discriminate against Brazil's minorities – such as her transgender wife.
"I'm here because I believe in democracy," she told the AFP news agency. "Because I'm scared."
Witnesses reported that the march was notably more crowded and animated than President Lula's rally on the same street on Friday, the culmination of a lackluster campaign ahead of the election.
After the third, fourth and fifth places all went to right-wing candidates, who polled over eight million votes between them, Lula and the left appear to have a mountain to climb in the run-off.

The incumbent's campaign has shifted its focus to social media, where the far-right dominates but Lula has largely been absent, arguing he "like[s] to say only what is essential." But on Wednesday, the president convened leftist influencers who won legislative seats on Sunday to advise his campaign.

articles.title: Winnipeg sex offender who flew under family's radar by changing name gets 15 years for abusing child
articles.summary: A convicted sex offender who sexually abused a 13-year-old boy whose family didn't know about the man's criminal past because he'd changed his name has been sentenced to 15 years in prison.

image.caption: Ryan James Knight, seen here in a 2024 photo, was sentenced in Winnipeg on Wednesday. He was convicted earlier this year of sexual interference and making child sexual abuse and exploitation material. (Submitted by Danielle Gzebb)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New
A convicted sex offender who sexually abused a 13-year-old boy whose family didn't know about the man's criminal past because he'd changed his name has been sentenced to 15 years in prison.
Ryan Knight 'leaving a trail of trauma' behind him, judge says
WARNING: This article contains details of child sexual abuse.
Ryan James Knight pleaded guilty in July to sexual interference and making child sexual abuse and exploitation material from August 2024 to March 2025.

Court heard Wednesday the boy's family had hired Knight, who was in his early 40s at the time, to renovate their basement. Knight then ended up hiring the child to do odd jobs around his own home down the street, where the repeated abuse happened.

Several years before, Knight had changed his last name from Gabourie. That meant that when the boy's family tried to look into Knight, they didn't find that he'd been convicted roughly two decades earlier of breaking into children's homes and sexually assaulting them as their families slept.
"They were duped," provincial court Judge Kael McKenzie said as he handed down Knight's sentence, after a joint recommendation from lawyers.
"It's not just one person that you hurt. It's over and over and over again, and for a long time…. You're just leaving a trail of trauma behind you, and for decades now."

The abuse came to light after Knight was out driving in a truck with the boy after midnight in March 2025, and ended up being pulled over by police. When officers found Knight had no familial relationship with the boy, they started an investigation that eventually uncovered Knight had been repeatedly sexually abusing the child.
Undated pictures of Knight released by Manitoba Justice in January 2024. (Manitoba Justice)

The boy, who can't be identified because of a publication ban, told police Knight would take him to the movies and let him sleep over at his house, and that he occasionally lent the boy a cellphone and let him play on his computer, an agreed statement of facts read by Crown attorney Katie Dojack said.

Investigators later seized electronics from Knight, which revealed child sexual abuse images of the boy. That led to police notifying the boy's parents that he'd been sexually assaulted and requesting to speak with him. The boy agreed but asked that his parents not be provided his video statement to watch.

The boy told police he didn't initially disclose anything to Child and Family Services when they became involved because he didn't trust them and "worried they would tell his dad," the agreed facts said.

items: Man charged with sexual assault of 2 teen boys after families built 'trusting relationship' with him: police

blocks.text: "He told police that he was embarrassed to talk about the accused and that the accused had warned him not to tell anyone."
During the investigation, the boy also told police Knight used to have another boy "hanging out with him." That child was later confirmed to be 14.

That boy's mother told police she'd known Knight for nine years, and her son occasionally slept over at his home. However, she cut off contact when her family members raised concerns and she noticed the boy was "behaving differently."
While police initially said Knight was charged with sexually abusing two teens, court records show other charges against him were stayed.
Light in boy's eyes 'replaced by anger'
The father of the boy whose son Knight was convicted of abusing said the boy, "who once openly showed his love for his family, has changed."
"Since what happened to him, he has often expressed anger toward us, and the light in his eyes seems to have been replaced by anger," the father wrote in a victim impact statement Dojack read.
"We hope that he will regain that spark, but we do not know whether he will."
He said while he searched Knight's name online before hiring him, he only found one complaint about a job he'd done.
"I believe his change of last name prevented me from discovering that history," the father said.

items: Brandon man sentenced to 25 years for sexual abuse of foster children

blocks.text: The boy's grandmother said she watched her grandson change from "a happy-go-lucky child into a very angry and sullen child."

"I watched the sparkly twinkle in his eyes disappear," she wrote in her victim impact statement. "He didn't believe we could help him, because Ryan had convinced him that his family didn't care about him and wouldn't believe him."
Prosecutor Dojack said sexual victimization can be especially shameful for boys "because of social expectations that males are supposed to appear tough."
"Embarrassment, humiliation and homophobia form a particularly toxic and stigmatizing combination for male child victims," she said. "I think that is certainly something to be considered here."
Knight's lawyer, Theodore Mariash, told court his client's childhood was also marked by "horrific abuse."
When given the chance to speak for himself, Knight apologized for the harm he caused to people sitting in the courtroom gallery and for taking away their right to know about his past.

items: 'No shame in being a victim': lawyer, social worker confront childhood abuser in court during sentencing
Man sentenced to 25 years for 'horrendous' sexual abuse after survivors spoke out

blocks.text: "I can't even imagine what it's like to learn who you had sitting at your dinner table," he said from the prisoner's box. "And I'm really sorry for that. No one deserved anything I have done."

Court heard Knight has a little over 13 years left on his sentence, with enhanced credit for time served. He's also subject to a list of conditions, including not contacting either of the children mentioned in the agreed facts.

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​

articles.title: Alberta premier says ‘ridiculous’ for separatists to offer royalties, water to Americans
articles.summary: Premier Danielle Smith says it was “absurd” and “ridiculous” for prominent separatists to offer the United States government access to fresh water and resource royalties in return for its help…

image.caption: Premier Danielle Smith joined federal Defence Minister David McGuinty for an announcement at CFB Edmonton on Wednesday. (Sam Martin/CBC News)

blocks.text: Edmonton

Premier Danielle Smith says it was “absurd” and “ridiculous” for prominent separatists to offer the United States government access to fresh water and resource royalties in return for its help establishing an independent Alberta.
Danielle Smith says U.S. government needs to deal with elected Canadian governments
The information was reported by the Globe and Mail on Saturday. CBC News has not independently confirmed the details in the story.
Alberta separatists met three times with U.S. State Department officials in Washington in late 2025.
“I think it's absurd that anybody would offer something like that up that's not theirs to offer,” Smith said at an unrelated news conference in Edmonton Wednesday.
“It's a decision that Albertans would make, and I don't think Albertans would support it.”
The Washington meetings were already public knowledge, but what was offered to U.S. officials was new information.

items: Past Alberta separatist meetings in U.S. don't fall under foreign influence registry: watchdog

blocks.text: According to the Globe and Mail, Dennis Modry, co-founder of the pro-independence Alberta Prosperity Project (APP), told the media outlet about the offer that was made.
Jeff Rath, a lawyer with the separatist movement, denied to the Globe and Mail that any of those matters were discussed.
Mitch Sylvestre is the president for the Bonnyville-Cold Lake UCP constituency association. He also heads up the APP.

In an interview with The Canadian Press on Monday, he also denied any discussion about access to water or oil taking place during the meetings in Washington, though he noted he only went to one meeting.
"We have no authority to do any of that," he said.
"We're not in government. We can't go down there and have that conversation."
Sylvestre added that he believes there's enough support in Alberta for independence that U.S. support is not needed.

items: It's the biggest Alberta separatist account on the internet. It has links to a movement leader

blocks.text: Smith has been criticized for including a question on Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum about whether the province should remain in Canada or if it should start the legal process for a binding future referendum that would provide a definitive answer on Alberta’s fate within Confederation.
Smith didn’t answer a question Wednesday about whether she believes she has encouraged U.S. involvement in the political situation by asking the question.
Instead she said she believes the people that were involved in the meetings are critics of hers because she plans to vote to stay in Canada.
“We expect that the American administration will deal with the duly elected governments,” Smith added.
“That includes mine, but it also includes the government of Canada.”
Alberta mayors voice concern ahead of fall referendum
The mayors of Calgary and Edmonton appeared on CBC News Network's Power & Politics on Monday and spoke about their concerns in light of the Globe and Mail report.
Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said he believes the referendum is a distraction from other issues facing Albertans.
He said he's worried about the potential for misinformation and foreign interference, and more generally about the impact that Alberta's referendum could have on the province's future.
"My fear is regardless of the outcome, this is not going to be settled," he said.
"My fear is that we're going to continue to see continued divisive debates and potentially more referendums being called."

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said the report about water and royalties being offered to the U.S. is a reminder of what's at risk, especially with U.S. President Donald Trump's past comments about his interest in potentially making Canada his country's 51st state.
"That to me has been part of the challenge of this," he said. "This is a very dangerous path."
Knack said he believes the vast majority of Edmontonians do not support a binding referendum on independence, and called on all Albertans to vote in this month's referendum.

"If there's one good thing about this ridiculous story — I can't even believe that's happening — is that hopefully it serves as a wake-up call to everyone in this province that you cannot be sleeping on Oct. 19."
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: U.S. army moves to execute man convicted in 2009 deadly Fort Hood rampage by firing squad
articles.summary: The former U.S. army officer convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad in December in what would be the first U.S.…

image.caption: U.S. Maj. Nidal Hasan, the army psychiatrist who was convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting rampage, is seen in a booking photo in April 2010. The U.S. army is moving to execute Hasan by firing squad in December. (Bell County Sheriff's Office/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The former U.S. army officer convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad in December in what would be the first U.S. military execution in more than 65 years.
Few details have been released about who would be part of the firing squad or what procedure they would use

Acting secretary of the U.S. army Adam Telle said in a social media post that army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood. This followed news from the Pentagon that U.S. President Donald Trump had approved the execution.

The announcement stunned an attorney who had represented Hasan in a civil case, and raised concerns among experts on military law about whether the army followed its mandated process for setting an execution and notifying a prisoner they've been condemned to death.

It also sparked questions about how a firing squad would be assembled and what procedure it would use. The last time the military executed someone by firing squad was shortly after the Second World War.
Here's a look at the military execution process and how experts say this case may proceed.

A man and child lay flowers and a balloon outside the front gate of the Fort Hood Army Post in Fort Hood, Texas following the shooting rampage which left 13 people dead in 2009. (Jessica Rinaldi/Reuters)
Who would form firing squad

Telle confirmed in his post on X that Trump had approved the execution on Oct. 2, starting the clock in army regulations that requires an execution date to be set no sooner than 60 days and no later than 150 days after that approval.

Telle also noted that the execution would be carried out by firing squad, but did not offer details of where on base the execution would take place, what personnel would be a part of that squad or what procedure they would follow.

The Associated Press asked both Pentagon officials and the army for more details, but those requests were declined. A message to the army seeking comment on the potential procedural issues was sent Wednesday.

The procedures for execution in army regulations do not contain specific protocols for particular methods of execution. Experts said in previous iterations of the firing squad — nearly 80 years ago — one shooter would be given a blank so they all could plausibly believe they had not fired the fatal shot.
The execution could be delayed

Hasan, an army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups, shouted Allahu akbar — Arabic for "God is greater" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.

He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims — a defence a military judge barred him from presenting during his trial. Hasan made almost no effort to defend himself in court, telling jurors when he acted as his own counsel that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides."

"What happens now, is if Dr. Hasan decides he wants to resist execution, he can go to federal civilian court for a Habeas Corpus petition … and that can last years," said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
Habeas Corpus is a legal procedure whereby an incarcerated person can challenge the lawfulness of their imprisonment.
"It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions," Fidell said.

items: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan sentenced to death
Hasan guilty in Fort Hood U.S. army massacre

blocks.text: Trump resumed the federal death penalty after an informal moratorium during previous administrations. The federal government executed 13 people between 2020 and early 2021, contributing to making Trump the most prolific execution president in over 130 years.
Military executions rare

Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system and executions even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., and the last execution that took place there was a hanging in 1961.

John Galligan, a retired colonel and a former military judge, represented Hasan in civil matters. The attorney said Wednesday that he's limited on what he can talk about, but called the rush to conduct the execution "horrific."

items: Fort Hood massacre trial a rare U.S. military execution case

blocks.text: Galligan, who spoke with Hasan on Wednesday, said he believes the army regulation to have the facility's army commandant notify Hasan, accompanied by a chaplain and a Trial Defence Service attorney or civilian counsel if possible, was not followed. Galligan said that, according to Hasan, there was no legal counsel present.

"For the life of me, I don't know what they are trying to accomplish in such a rush fashion … and by trying to conduct this execution at Fort Hood, when he has such medical issues," Galligan said, raising questions about how Hasan, who is paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair, would be transported to Fort Hood.
How South Carolina conducts firing squads

Before Hasan's execution was set for Fort Hood, there was speculation the army might reach out to one of the handful of states that have recently reinstated the firing squad for use in executions — particularly South Carolina or Utah, where they've renovated facilities and established protocols.
South Carolina has killed three prisoners by firing squad in the past 18 months, the only such executions in the U.S. in the past 16 years.

It's unclear if the army will borrow from the state's protocol, but it sets out for three volunteer shooters to stand 4.6 metres from the condemned prisoner, who is strapped to a chair. A medical professional uses an X-ray to find the prisoner's heart and place a target over it. A hood is placed over the prisoner's head after his final words, and a shade is lifted so the shooters can see their target.
All three shooters have live ammunition and fire at the same time with no verbal warning for the condemned prisoner.
South Carolina spent about $54,000 US to renovate its death chamber for the firing squad.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Palace: DOH ‘closely monitoring’ plague concerns in Russia
articles.summary: The plague concerns came following the death of a laboratory technician in Russia who was working at a plague research institute.

blocks.text: This photo shows a woman walking past the logo of Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's consumer and health watchdog in Moscow on October 5, 2026.
AFP / Igor Ivanko

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang assured the public on Wednesday, October 7, that the Department of Health (DOH) has started to monitor the plague risk in Russia, although international health officials said there were no signs of an outbreak.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said at a press briefing in Singapore that the state’s health department is following the recommendations of the World Health Organization (WHO) regarding concerns about the plague.

“Rest assured po sa mga kababayan natin po na nakatutok po ang DOH at kung ano man po ang kinakailangan pang gawin, ‘yun po ay kanilang gagawin. So far ay nami-meet naman po nila ang mga requirements para maibsan ang takot natin tungkol dito sa plague na nangyayari sa Russia,” Castro said.

(Rest assured, our fellow countrymen, that the DOH is focused on the concerns, and whatever needs to be done, they will do that. So far, they are meeting the requirements to relieve our fears about the reported plague in Russia.)
The plague concerns came following the death of a laboratory technician in Russia who was working at a plague research institute.
Authorities are investigating whether the lab technician died of pneumonic plague, raising global concerns.
The WHO, however, stressed that there is no need to be alarmed as no signs of a wider outbreak were detected.
Plague refers to an infectious disease primarily affecting rodents and micromammals and is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague, which is the most dangerous form of plague, infects the lungs and can be transmitted from person to person through droplets released from breathing, coughing, or sneezing.

articles.title: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
articles.summary: The skipper who led India to the historic 2025 World Cup win has stepped down from her role in all three formats.

blocks.text: When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India.
India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan.
That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later.

Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport.
Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats.

Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless.

Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience.
The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana.

In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer.
Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago.

Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world.
Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped.
Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains.

Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on.
Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post.
"I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote.
"Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again.
"Captaincy ends, the journey continues."
Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future.

In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision.

The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket.

Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones.
Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age.
Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai.
The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development.
She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since.
An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills.

Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome.
That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name.

The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history.

Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup.

Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 as was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals.
India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket.
With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate.

articles.title: Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa
articles.summary: Wicknell Chivayo divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.

blocks.text: Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.

He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes.

He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving.

Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes.

His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune. His detractors recoiled at the ostentatious displays, questioned the origins of his money and his political connections, and saw his lifestyle as a stark illustration of inequality.

But Chivayo remained tone-deaf to such criticism. As his fortunes rose, he became ever more unapologetic about flaunting his wealth in a country where nearly half the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank.

"He gave to those few on an island of wealth in a sea of poverty," Pedzisai Ruhanya, director of the Zimbabwe Democracy Institute think-tank, told the BBC, explaining how his donations were mainly to influential people.
He dismissed Chivayo's generosity as grandstanding for the ruling Zanu-PF party - an attempt to ensure the support of key politicians and even church leaders.
Nonetheless, there has been an outpouring of grief, especially from recipients of his largesse, and tributes from politicians, religious leaders and business figures.

Among the mourners gathered at the Chivayos' opulent home in the capital, Harare, ahead of their burial on Thursday, was Cleopas Mukungunugwa, a young and prominent Zanu-PF social media influencer and recipient of two luxury cars from Sir Wicknell.

Standing outside the mansion, where a massive poster of the couple is displayed, he told local media that he was devastated by his patron's death, external, explaining how "Sir Wicknell" often dictated what he should write in his posts.
"He was criticised by many on social media and our goal was to bolster his reputation as a philanthropist," he said.
Chivayo dropped out of high school aged 15 because his family could no longer afford the fees after his father died when he was 10.

His first job was as a wages clerk for a bus company. From there, he moved into his first independent hustle - selling mobile phones and dealing in foreign currency, often on the black market at the height of the country's hyperinflation crisis.

In 2005, he was sentenced to five years in prison for money laundering involving 837,000 South African rand (then worth $137,500, £72,000). He served three years at Chikurubi Maximum Prison after two years were suspended.

Details of his career following his release are murky, but he went into the energy business, becoming what one state-run newspaper described as a "tenderpreneur" -making money by getting government contracts.

He headed the firm Intratrek Zimbabwe, which partnered with Chinese electrical giant CHiNT Electric. This was at a time when legislation required all companies in the country to cede economic control to black Zimbabweans, under a policy known as indigenisation.

In 2014, Intratrek was selected to build a 100MW solar power station in the southern town of Gwanda. A contract worth more than $170m was signed the following year. It became one of the biggest controversies of Chivayo's business career.
Zimbabwe Power Company, the state-owned utility that awarded the contract, sought to terminate it when Intratrek failed to deliver, but the courts ultimately ruled that the agreement remained valid.
A parliamentary inquiry later described Intratrek as a "briefcase company" being used as a front to attract investment.
Chivayo acknowledged that Intratrek lacked expertise in solar construction, describing it as the local partner while CHiNT provided the technical muscle.
Intratrek received an advance of more than $5m for the Gwanda solar plant, but it remains unbuilt to this day.
Just weeks before Chivayo's death, Intratrek received a government notice to proceed with the project and was given 24 months to complete it.

As the accusations flew, the businessman just smiled and sweet-talked his way through the maelstrom - even winning over President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was initially unimpressed by him when he first came to power.

In 2018, Mnangagwa cited Gwanda as a lesson in the dangers of doing business with "fly-by-night briefcase businessmen", adding ominously that "Chikurubi is not full". The state-run Herald newspaper reported that the warning was directed at Chivayo.

Yet within a few years, that relationship transformed into a bromance. In one of several photographs capturing the remarkable informality between them, Chivayo lounges, almost lying, on a sofa beside Mnangagwa, apparently entirely at ease in the president's company.
His access was not confined to Zanu-PF - he also posted photographs with opposition figures, including the late Morgan Tsvangirai and Nelson Chamisa.
But he became a conspicuous presence around Mnangagwa, speaking glowingly of the president and making no secret of his support for Zanu-PF.
He faced allegations over the procurement of materials for the 2023 elections, in which Mnangagwa was voted in for a second term.

Investigations alleged that South African supplier Ren-Form grossly inflated prices and subsequently paid hundreds of millions of rand to a company linked to him. Chivayo denied wrongdoing, and Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission later said it had found no evidence linking him to procurement fraud. Ren-Form denied any wrongdoing.

In April, he offered the country's 360 legislators $10,000 each, prompting accusations that he wanted to influence an impending vote on a controversial constitutional amendment to extend what would have been Mnangagwa's final five-year term by two years to 2030.
He was forced to withdraw the offer following a backlash and denied it was intended to influence the vote.

When the legislation was signed into law several months later, Zanu-PF posted a video clip of him with the caption, external: "Billionaire Sir Wicknell Chivayo celebrates… singing '2030 Ndeya Emmerson Baba!' while cruising at 51,000 feet aboard his Gulfstream G550".

Access to power became part of Chivayo's social-media persona. In June, Eswatini's King Mswati III granted him citizenship of the southern African kingdom and a diplomatic passport - photographs and videos showed him kneeling before the monarch, external.

He had an impressive camera roll, with snaps of him posing with other African presidents such as Nigeria's Bola Tinubu, external, Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, external, Malawi's Peter Mutharika, external, Mozambique's Daniel Chapo, external, Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema, external and he was part of the delegation that met South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa, external when he visited Mnangagwa's farm earlier this year.
Some relationships extended beyond formal meetings. In August, Chivayo and his wife attended the engagement of Kenyan President William Ruto's daughter Charlene at the president's family home.

Afterwards, Ruto personally drove the couple to their waiting helicopter. Chivayo filmed the journey from the passenger seat, external. True to form, he gloated: "Being driven by the president of the republic. God is the greatest."
Ruto wrote on X following the death, external: "I will remember him for his friendship, his energy, and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent."
But in Kenya the Zimbabwean businessman was viewed with great suspicion because of his closeness to Ruto - something expressed loudly on social media since his death.

Many of the comments are not printable but as Kenyan blogger Cyprian Nyakundi put it, external, listing some of the controversies surrounding Chivayo: "As a Kenyan, I distance myself completely from President Ruto's glowing tribute to Wicknell Chivayo. Those condolences and that 'dear friend' language are his own, not mine, as a Kenyan."
One commentator on X said his death had "united Africans in celebration", external.
"When a man's passing brings more relief than sorrow, the reaction itself tells a powerful story. It is time for those in power to reflect and reevaluate!"
At home there has also been pushback against those who say speaking ill of the dead is un-African - as the topic of the tycoon's death is the trending topic in Zimbabwe these days.
At a shopping centre in Harare over the weekend, Christabel Moyo voiced what many have been saying.
"What is African - getting rich from inflated state contracts and using that money to support Zanu-PF?" the 42-year-old accountant asked.
"He was busy doling out cars and cash to the rich while the Zimbabwean public health system is collapsing."

The extraordinary gifting spree for which he will be remembered began around 2023. Musicians, sports and business figures, politicians and religious leaders were among the beneficiaries of cars and cash in what some might see as a blatant attempt to buy support for the ruling party.
He started with relatively modest Toyota Aquas, but the gifts soon became dramatically more expensive.
Top musician Jah Prayzah, who is close to Zanu-PF was given three luxury cars, along with about $400,000, over three years.
The musician postponed his wedding - scheduled to take place last weekend - because of the helicopter crash, saying: "Wicknell was more than a friend to us."
Another key recipient was Bishop Nehemiah Mutendi, head of the Zion Christian Church that is fiercely loyal to Zanu-PF. The cleric received millions in cash donations and four luxury cars.
Chivayo regularly attended the Johane Masowe weChishanu African apostolic church, one of the biggest in Zimbabwe, whose followers can often be seen worshipping outdoors wearing white robes.

It also received scores of cars, buses and cash from the businessman as he pushed the influential sect closer to the ruling party, taking along Mnangagwa as guest of honour to a massive church gathering in August.
But not everyone accepted Chivayo's largesse. Eunor Guti, widow of Zimbabwe Assemblies of God Africa founder Archbishop Ezekiel Guti, declined a luxury vehicle and $250,000 in cash.

In 2024, veteran musician and government critic Thomas Mapfumo, who is based in the US, rejected Chivayo's offer of a luxury car and house, saying he could not be "bribed" and later describing his money as "dirty".
However, this year, he did accept $1m to perform at Jah Prayzah's wedding and Chivayo's birthday party in November.

Some long-time admirers of Mapfumo, who arrived in Harare on the eve of the helicopter crash, accused him on social media of compromising his principles, though this was denied by the 81-year-old musician.
Chivayo's generosity was not confined to individuals - he also donated 20 ambulances to Zimbabwe's failing public health system and gave buses and other assistance to schools.

Those close to him say his philanthropy was not always performed for an audience. Prominent lawyer Wilson Manase said following the tycoon's death that when he had fallen seriously ill in Dubai, Chivayo flew over to visit him.
In an interview with state broadcaster ZBC, the lawyer, who was promised a car in Chivayo's last tweet, described him as "pure hearted" and deeply religious.
The tycoon had two young children with his first wife Sonja Madzikanda, from whom he split in 2024 and was still embroiled in a messy court case over the divorce settlement.

He was also keen not to forget his roots. On the day he died, he had visited his rural home in Gandami, south-east of Harare, where he was building a $1m eight-bedroom mansion to be officially opened in November for his birthday.

He boasted it would bring "Borrowdale Brooke to Gandami" - a reference to one of Harare's most exclusive residential estates. He had also pledged $500,000 to improve the local primary and secondary schools and a clinic.
Chivayo's death leaves Zanu-PF without one of its most colourful campaigners.

But he also leaves behind unanswered questions - with many of his countrymen continuing to wonder how exactly he rose from such humble beginnings to becoming a multi-millionaire with the means to dole out such extravagant gifts.
Ish Mafundikwa is a freelance journalist based in Harare

articles.title: New York court hears arguments in ongoing 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: The families allege that men with links to the Saudi government helped those who carried out the 2001 attacks, something the country denies.

blocks.text: Bayoumi, who is now retired from government work, has denied knowing the two men were hijackers or that he had any involvement in 9/11, while Saudi Arabia has said that any allegation that it or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.
The Kingdom has argued that, as a foreign sovereign state, it has immunity from prosecution in US courts.
The families, who first filed the lawsuit in 2002, spent several years lobbying US Congress to pass an amendment to the foreign sovereign immunity law to allow the case to go ahead.

In 2016, Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), which allows civil claims against a foreign state or official for injuries, death, or damages from an act of international terrorism.
In August 2025, the Manhattan District Court ruled that the 9/11 families had presented enough evidence to meet the terms of the act and the case was allowed to proceed towards a trial.
Saudi Arabia on Wednesday asked the Court of Appeals to reverse that decision.

Counsel Gregory Rapawy argued core issues of fact – including the central question of the nature of Bayoumi's employment by the Saudi state – had not been decided and needed to be done so before the country could be stripped of immunity.
9/11 families' lawyer Gavin Simpson argued that the District Court had already found that Bayoumi's actions "were not just acts of a good Samaritan or an innocent participant".
"He was, in fact, following Saudi Arabia's instructions when assisting the hijackers," said Simpson, and that these were points that Saudi Arabia had "failed to rebut."
One option the judges seemed to wrestle with was whether to send the case back to the district court to make more concrete findings, which could involve taking testimony from live witnesses.

Asked by Judge Guido Calabresi which witnesses Saudi Arabia could call in that eventuality, Rapawy suggested that if the issue ultimately came down to Bayoumi's credibility, "we would have to see" if he could be called to testify.
As he drew the hearing to a close, Judge William Nardini said "it's a difficult case, and we will take it under advisement", meaning that the panel would issue a ruling at a future date.
Speaking outside the courthouse, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom was killed in the World Trade Center, told the BBC she felt positive about the hearing.

"25 years is an extraordinary time to go without accountability and justice for the murder of your loved one. What we hope is that the judges will uphold [District Court] Judge Daniels' decision and move to a trial."

articles.title: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
articles.summary: The new charges are expected to accuse Maduro and his wife of playing a role in the torture of Americans in Venezuelan prisons, US media reports.

blocks.text: Federal prosecutors are expected to bring additional charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, the BBC's US media partner CBS has reported.
The new charges accuse them of playing a role in the torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to CBS.

US forces seized Maduro and Flores from their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in a dramatic, night-time raid on 3 January, and brought them to New York to face charges for alleged weapon and drug offences, which they deny.
The BBC has contacted Maduro's lawyer for comment as well as the US Attorney's office in Manhattan ​which brought the charges.
Additional people may be charged for their role in torturing more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government under Maduro, CBS reports.
Maduro's attorney, Barry Pollack, told CBS that he was not provided notice about any additional charges.
Flores, who is facing drug trafficking and weapons charges, is scheduled to appear in federal court for a bond hearing on Thursday in New York.
The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027.
The US has accused Maduro of narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and possession of and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
He and 14 others were first indicted in 2020, during President Trump's first term.
Prosecutors have alleged that Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices engaged in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnered with cartels designated as terrorist groups.
They said the accused "abused their positions of public trust and corrupted once-legitimate institutions to import tons of cocaine into the United States".
Maduro has previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.

He and his wife's lawyers have asked the court to dismiss the charges because he is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. The judge has not ruled on their requests.

articles.title: Lawyer accused of fraud says bad cheque didn't hurt the bank
articles.summary: The fraud trial for a suspended Ontario lawyer ping-ponged back and forth on whether TD Bank had suffered any harm or risk of loss as a result of a bad cheque the lawyer wrote.

image.caption: Suspended lawyer Nicholas Julian Cartel, accused of fraud for writing a bad cheque to allegedly cover a shortfall in his law firm's trust account, leaves a downtown Toronto courthouse on Monday during a break in his criminal trial. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

blocks.text: The fraud trial for a suspended Ontario lawyer ping-ponged back and forth Tuesday on whether TD Bank had suffered any harm or risk of loss as a result of a bad cheque the lawyer wrote.

Nicholas Cartel, a class-action and litigation specialist, is on trial on a single count of fraud over $5,000 relating to a $300,000 personal cheque he wrote in 2023, which prosecutors allege was done to help cover up the financial collapse of his and his wife’s law firm. That cheque bounced five days after being deposited into a TD bank account belonging to the law firm.

In the second day of testimony in provincial court in Toronto, a witness representing TD was grilled by both the defence and prosecution about what harm, if any, the bank incurred as a result. Proving fraud under the Criminal Code requires proving that someone either suffered a loss or was exposed to a risk of economic deprivation.
“There was no negative balance at the end of the day?” Cartel asked TD employee Tonya Cole in cross-examination.
“That’s correct, yes,” Cole replied.
Prosecutors Megan Rauser, left, and Dihim Emami converse outside court at the end of the first day of Cartel's criminal trial. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

Cartel has not denied he wrote the bad cheque for $300,000 on a personal account at RBC — which he maintains was a joint account with his wife, Singa Bui. But he says his wife, not he, deposited the cheque to the TD trust account of their firm, Cartel & Bui LLP. And then she was the one, he says, who immediately after obtained a $2.2-million certified cheque from TD to send to a client of the firm.

Prosecutors allege the certified cheque couldn’t have been issued without the top-up from the $300,000 deposit, because the law firm’s trust account was already in shortfall. Bui had been embezzling money from it for years, according to her own evidence in a separate civil case.
When Cartel’s personal cheque from RBC bounced five days later, TD had to go into his firm’s trust account and take out the $300,000.
Prosecutor Dihim Emami focused on that in his re-examination of Cole.

“It's fortuitous that this account had funds subsequent for TD to recover their $300,000, correct?” he asked. “If this account was depleted … or for a whole host of reasons other influxes of money didn't come in, TD might never have recovered that amount, correct?”
“That's possible, yes,” Cole said.
Home buyers and sellers left in lurch

The collapse of Cartel & Bui LLP in December 2023 left more than 25 home buyers and sellers in southern Ontario in the lurch for amounts ranging from $66,000 up to $2.16 million, in the case of one couple — money they had either transferred to the firm's trust account to buy a home or were expecting in payouts after selling their home.

Bui has admitted in lawsuits against her and Cartel that she started pilfering money from the firm’s trust account as far back as 2014 to fund the couple’s "luxury lifestyle," in a Ponzi-like scheme where incoming funds from new clients would cover for amounts she had stolen. She and Cartel bought two Toronto homes for $6 million total, sent their children to private school, took "luxurious vacations" and, she said, “decorated our home and office with elegant furnishings and expensive art.”

Cartel has long maintained he didn’t know about the embezzlement until December 2023, but a Superior Court judge overseeing more than 15 lawsuits against the couple and their former law firm has questioned those claims, saying at one point in June 2024: “Did she pay for nice gifts for you? Did you buy a car that she paid for? Did she pay mortgage payments? How can you not know, when you're living with her and you've got a home together and you've got children together, where $6 million went?"
The judge later sent both Cartel and Bui to jail, for 30 days and 20 days respectively, for contempt, ruling that they "have taken active steps to hide their finances and to frustrate the court."

Now-disbarred real estate lawyer Singa Bui leaves a Toronto courthouse in October 2024 after being sentenced to 30 days in provincial prison for civil contempt of court. The sentence was later reduced to 20 days. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

A Law Society of Ontario ruling in April 2024 suspending Cartel from practising law commented that “while it is conceivable that Ms. Bui acted alone and that Mr. Cartel had no knowledge or involvement, there are good reasons to believe otherwise,” including that various of Cartel’s explanations were “difficult to accept.”
Bui has since been disbarred while the Law Society’s disciplinary case against Cartel has yet to come to a final hearing.
Bogus signatures
In his criminal trial, Cartel is representing himself after a falling-out with his former defence lawyer Richard Posner.

Court records from a separate case, where Cartel challenged Posner’s invoices, show Posner criticizing Cartel for being “arrogant and patronizing” toward staff at Posner’s firm. Posner also told Cartel he was “completely uncomfortable” with Cartel’s wish to interact mainly over email “given the tenor of your writing.” Cartel had made claims in emails to Posner's firm that, among other things, the prosecution in his case had drafted a fraudulent document to pressure Cartel into agreeing to certain facts ahead of trial.

Cartel, in turn, accused Posner of “deliberate willful blindness” to documents that would supposedly help exonerate him. He also said Posner’s assistant “forced condescending, unsolicited opinions of culpability onto” him.

In another email, Posner states that if Cartel is going to testify in his own defence, it will take “a few days” to coach him because “without extensive preparation, Mr. Cartel will not present well as a witness.”

items: Lawyer couple accused of stealing millions from homebuyers while law society stalled
Lawyers at centre of $7M real estate embezzlement case charged with fraud

blocks.text: The dispute between them also reveals that Cartel put together documents that contained bogus signatures of another lawyer, George Tsimiklis. The signatures appear on the witness line of two affidavits Cartel swore in his dispute with Posner.

“Although the document bears my signature … I did not sign it either in person or electronically, and I did not authorize Mr. Cartel or any other person to affix or reproduce my signature on it,” Tsimiklis says in his own sworn statement filed in the case.
Cartel says the documents were only in draft form and he never intended them to be submitted to court.
Tsimiklis was a colleague of Cartel and has previously witnessed affidavits for him and represented Cartel’s wife, Bui.

Cartel told CBC during a break in his trial on Monday that he emailed the documents to a court clerk but only as drafts and he wasn’t formally filing them. He blamed the clerk for misunderstanding instructions and placing the affidavits with the bogus signatures into the court file.

items: Lawyer who admitted stealing millions of dollars from homeowners is disbarred

blocks.text: Asked how the signatures got onto his affidavits in the first place, Cartel claimed it happened because different pages from different documents got compiled together by the court clerk, including some pages that had Tsimiklis’s genuine signature from past filings.
That explanation, however, doesn’t square with the fact that Tsimiklis’s bogus signatures don’t appear on their own page but rather at the bottom of the newly created affidavits.
Cartel is currently suing CBC, Toronto Life magazine and the Toronto Sun newspaper for their coverage of his and his wife’s ordeals.
His trial is scheduled to resume in November.

articles.title: 'Unimaginable loss': Horses killed on B.C. highway while travelling to championship
articles.summary: Four horses were travelling from across Western Canada to compete in the Equestrian Canada National Dressage West championship in Langley. Three were killed in a crash, and another was injured.

image.caption: Mackenzie Abbott is seen beside Fearless, a horse that was killed during a highway crash in B.C. while travelling to the National Dressage and Para Dressage Championships West in Langley on Oct. 6, 2026. (Submitted by Amelia Carter)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Four horses were travelling from across Western Canada to compete in the Equestrian Canada National Dressage West championship in Langley. Three were killed in a crash, and another was injured.
Police say the driver hit a rock wall on Highway 1 in southeast B.C.; 3 horses killed and 1 injured in crash
The Canadian equestrian community is mourning the death of three horses after a collision in B.C.
The horses were travelling from Manitoba and Alberta to Langley on Monday, to compete in the 2026 Equestrian Canada National Dressage West championship at the Thunderbird Show Park.
At 8:45 a.m. local time on Oct. 6, officers with the B.C. Highway Patrol responded to a single-vehicle crash roughly 40 kilometres east of Revelstoke on Highway 1.
The driver was towing a trailer with four horses when she lost control and collided with a rock wall, according to Sgt. Michael McLaughlin.
Three horses died, and the fourth horse was injured.
Kate Wall seen with Rosaria, a dressage horse that died during a single vehicle collision on Highway 1 in B.C. on Oct. 6, 2026. (Shealynn Choy/S.C.apturing The Moment Photography)
Paramedics with B.C. Emergency Health Services responded to the crash with an ambulance.
"Paramedics provided emergency medical care to one patient, who was transported to hospital in stable condition," said BCEHS paramedic public information officer Brian Twaites.
Police said the driver was a 73-year-old woman from Langdon, Alta.
"The driver was issued a violation ticket for failing to keep right under the [B.C.] Motor Vehicle Act, which comes with a fine of $109," McLaughlin said.
Condolences from all over Canada are pouring in for the horses and those who knew them.
'My heart is completely shattered'
Mackenzie Abbott is a dressage rider and head trainer from Headingley, Man. She said two of the horses were ones she trained, and they were owned by Solace Stables.
"We have suffered an unimaginable loss and lost our beloved horses," Abbott said. "I loved my horses more than I could ever explain. My heart is completely shattered."
The two horses, named Fearless and Rosaria, were set to compete in Langley starting on Oct. 9.

Highway 1 near the Illecillewaet Brake Check, roughly near where the collision occurred on Oct. 6, 2026, east of Canyon Hot Springs and Revelstoke. Four horses were in the trailer and three died. (DriveBC)
"They were the top of their fields in our sport here in Manitoba, and we were looking forward to proving their capabilities to Canada," Abbott said.
The two horses were being transported with a driver, and Abbott had flown to Abbotsford to meet them at the competition. When she landed, she received a phone call about the crash.
"We all fundraised to get there," Abbott said. "We are just devastated to lose our best friends in the most tragic way."
The competition was being organized by Equestrian Canada, and is a major national event where athletes and their horses travel to the West Coast to compete.
It is common in the sport for athletes and owners to hire commercial drivers to transport the horses to the events.

items: Olympic champion Eric Lamaze to step away from role with Equestrian Canada

blocks.text: In a statement, Equestrian Canada said it has reached out to the athletes and owners involved and extended mental health support.
